practice.title: RAPID-FIRE
practice.afterTopic: AI app with RAG and streaming
items: Practise
practice.reference:
Forty short questions with sharp answers. Ten a day, out loud, under thirty seconds each. Speed
matters: these arrive in a burst, and hesitation reads as not knowing rather than as care.

**Practise**: read the question, answer immediately and out loud, then check. Score **2** (correct,
under 30s), **1** (correct but slow), **0** (blank or hedged). Any 1 is a rereading assignment; any
0 is a re-teach; confident-and-wrong is the worst case — trace the specific fact rather than
re-reading the topic.

Difficulty: 🟢 Beginner · **Must-know** · 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know** ·
🔴 Advanced · **Must-know** · ⚫ Expert

---

## JavaScript and TypeScript

**1. 🟢** What does `typeof null` return, and why can it not be fixed?
`"object"`. Values were originally tagged with a type and the null pointer's tag was `0`, which is
also the object tag — `Object(null)` returns `{}` for the same historical reason. Check with
`x === null`.

**2. 🟢** `==` versus `===` for `null`, `undefined`, `0`, `""`?
`===` compares type and value; `==` coerces, with nasty cases: `null == undefined` is true,
`null == 0` is false, `"" == 0` is true, and `NaN == NaN` is false. Use `===` plus explicit checks.

**3. 🟡** What does `Object.is` do that `===` does not?
Handles `NaN` (equal to itself) and distinguishes `+0` from `-0`. It is what `===` conceptually
should be.

**4. 🟢** Ways to copy an object, and what is shallow about each?
Spread, `Object.assign`, `structuredClone`. The first two are one level deep, so a nested object is
shared and mutating `copy.a.b` changes the original. `structuredClone` is deep and handles cycles,
Dates, and Maps, but throws on functions and DOM nodes.

**5. 🟡** What is a closure, and name a bug it causes?
A function plus its surrounding lexical environment. The classic bug: `var` in a `for` loop, where
every closure shares one binding, so all handlers see the final value. `let` per iteration fixes it
because each iteration gets its own binding.

**6. 🟡** What is the temporal dead zone?
The window between entering a scope and the `let`/`const` declaration being evaluated, where access
throws a `ReferenceError` instead of returning `undefined`. `var` has no TDZ — it is hoisted and
initialised to `undefined`.

**7. 🟢** What is hoisting?
Declarations are processed before execution: `var` and `function` declarations are hoisted and
available at the top of scope; `let`, `const`, and `class` are hoisted but stay in the TDZ until
their declaration runs.

**8. 🟡** Microtasks versus macrotasks?
Microtasks (promise callbacks, `queueMicrotask`, `MutationObserver`) drain completely before the next
macrotask. Macrotasks (`setTimeout`, I/O, events) run one at a time with the microtask queue drained
after each. Rendering happens between macrotasks, which is why an `await` loop still freezes the UI.

**9. 🟡** What is `requestIdleCallback`, and when is it the wrong tool?
Work during browser idle time with a deadline. Wrong for anything user-visible or time-sensitive:
idle time is not guaranteed and a busy page may never yield. Use it for analytics and prefetching.

**10. 🔴** `WeakMap` and `WeakSet` — what for, and why can you not iterate a `WeakMap`?
They hold references weakly, so keys can be collected — that is how you attach metadata to an object
without preventing collection, which a `Map` would turn into a real leak. They are not iterable
precisely because collection timing is nondeterministic. Keys must be objects.

**11. 🟡** What does `unknown` buy you over `any`?
It accepts anything on assignment but nothing can be used from it without narrowing, forcing a check.
`any` disables checking for the whole expression; `unknown` is the type-safe "anything".

**12. 🔴** Why is `Array<Dog>` not assignable to `Array<Animal>`, but a function taking `Dog` fits one
taking `Animal`?
Arrays are invariant because the type system protects writes: pushing a `Cat` into an `Array<Dog>`
reference would break it. Function *parameters* are contravariant — a function handling any `Animal`
can stand in for one handling only `Dog`, because everything you might pass it is a `Dog`.

**13. 🟡** What does `satisfies` do that an annotation does not?
It checks the value against a type without widening it; an annotation widens and discards the literal
shape. It is the difference between `{ id: 1 }` being inferred literally and being baked in.

**14. ⚫** Conditional types and `infer`, with a real use?
They let a type depend on another type. `type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T` — the
basis of most library utility types, and how you write a typed `deepReadonly`.

**15. 🟡** What does a discriminated union give you, and what is `never` for in the default branch?
It lets the compiler know which fields exist on which variant — `payload.at` is only accessible after
narrowing on `type`. The `never` default makes a switch that misses a variant a compile error, so
adding a variant surfaces every unhandled case.

---

## Browser and CSS

**16. 🟢** The three causes of layout shift?
An image or iframe without reserved dimensions, a font swap that changes metrics, and content injected
above existing content. Fix with `width`/`height` or `aspect-ratio`, a metric-adjusted fallback font
via `size-adjust`, and reserved space for anything async.

**17. 🟢** `grid` versus `flexbox`?
Grid is two-dimensional and for page structure — you define tracks and place items into cells. Flexbox
is one-dimensional, for a row or column along one axis. They compose: a grid page whose header is a
flex container is normal and good.

**18. 🟡** The box model?
Content, padding, border, margin, controlled by `box-sizing: border-box` (the sensible default). The
common bug is forgetting it, so padding and border add to a width you thought was fixed.

**19. 🟡** What is a stacking context, and name a bug it causes?
Any positioned element with `z-index` other than `auto`, an opacity below 1, a transform, a `filter`,
`will-change`, `contain: paint`, or a fixed element creates one. Inside it, `z-index` is scoped, so a
`z-index: 9999` header can end up *behind* a lower-indexed element outside the context. Fix by
flattening unnecessary contexts.

**20. 🟡** What is `content-visibility: auto` for, and what must it be paired with?
It skips rendering and layout for offscreen content. Pair it with `contain-intrinsic-size`, or the
scrollbar jumps around as content is measured.

**21. 🟢** How do you respect reduced motion?
`@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` to disable transitions and animations, and check it in JS
with `matchMedia` before anything imperative. Also stop scroll-triggered animation loops entirely —
motion that ignores the preference is an accessibility failure, not a preference failure.

**22. 🟡** What is `will-change` for, and what is the cost?
It hints that a property will change so the browser prepares a layer. The cost is GPU memory per
layer, and long-lived hints cause memory bloat. Use it shortly before the change and remove it after.

**23. 🟡** `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, cookies, IndexedDB?
`localStorage` is synchronous, string-only, origin-scoped, persists forever, and blocks the main
thread — fine for a theme, wrong for anything large. `sessionStorage` is the same but per tab.
Cookies are sent with requests (small size limit) and can be `HttpOnly`/`Secure`/`SameSite`, which is
why auth tokens go there. IndexedDB is asynchronous, structured, and large — for offline data and blobs.

**24. 🔴** The three longest tasks you would look for in a trace, and the fix for each?
Long tasks from synchronous JS or a huge layout/paint — chunk with `scheduler.yield()` and reduce DOM
work. Layout thrashing from interleaved layout reads and writes — batch reads then writes. A long
script from a large bundle — split and defer.

---

## HTTP and APIs

**25. 🟢** `401` versus `403` versus `404`?
`401`: I do not know who you are; here is how to authenticate. `403`: I know exactly who you are and
you may not do this. `404`: I will not tell you whether it exists — which avoids leaking existence to
an unauthorised caller.

**26. 🟡** What is a CORS preflight, and when does it happen?
For a non-simple request — anything but GET/HEAD/POST with simple headers and a simple content type —
the browser sends `OPTIONS` with `Access-Control-Request-Method` and headers, and the server must
answer with `Access-Control-Allow-*`. It does not happen for simple requests, so those are sent before
you know they will be blocked. CORS protects the *response* from scripts; it does not prevent a form
post.

**27. 🟡** What does `Vary` do?
It tells caches the response depends on a request header, so they store per-header variants. Omit
`Vary: Accept-Encoding` on a compressed response and you serve gzipped bytes to a client that cannot
decompress them. Also `Vary: Origin` for per-origin API responses.

**28. 🟡** `PUT` versus `PATCH`, and what must each be?
`PUT` replaces the resource at a known URI and **must** be idempotent — the same request ten times
leaves the same state. `PATCH` applies a partial modification and need not be idempotent. If a resource
has no meaningful URI, `PUT` to `/articles` with a client-generated id in the body stays idempotent.

**29. 🟡** What belongs in a `429` response?
A `Retry-After` header plus `RateLimit-Limit`, `-Remaining`, `-Reset`, and optionally a JSON body with
the same information and a machine-readable code. Consistent codes across endpoints matter more than
exact field names.

**30. 🔴** When is `OFFSET` pagination wrong?
When the table is being written to: inserts before your offset shift everything, so you skip and
repeat records. When the offset is deep, because the database still walks the skipped rows. Keyset
pagination fixes all three, at the cost of no random page access, and needs a stable, indexed, unique
sort key.

---

## Databases

**31. 🟢** What does a partial index do, and why is it useful?
It indexes only rows matching a predicate — `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`. Smaller, cheaper, more
specific than a full index, and often matched exactly by the query predicate so no filter step is
needed. A unique partial index also enforces uniqueness on a subset, which is how soft deletes are
handled.

**32. 🟡** Why might a composite index on `(a, b)` not be used for a query filtering only on `b`?
Leading-column rule: the index is sorted by `a` first, so rows with a given `b` are scattered across
the whole index. Reorder the columns to match the query or add an index on `b`.

**33. 🟡** What is an index-only scan, and what prevents it?
The index contains everything the query needs, so the heap is never visited. It requires a current
visibility map (recent vacuum) or Postgres still checks the heap for visibility. Covering indexes with
`INCLUDE` columns make it possible.

**34. 🟡** What is a deadlock, and how do you avoid it?
Two transactions holding locks the other needs. Avoid with consistent lock ordering across the
codebase, short transactions, a single atomic statement instead of read-then-write, and catching the
deadlock error to retry — Postgres detects and kills one automatically.

**35. 🔴** What is write skew, and how do you prevent it?
Two transactions each read overlapping state, take different decisions, and both commit, breaking a
joint invariant. Prevent with `SERIALIZABLE` (retry on `40001`), with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the rows
read, or by claiming the resource with a unique-constraint insert.

**36. ⚫** What does `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` tell you that `EXPLAIN` does not?
Actual row counts and timings, plus buffer reads and hits. It executes the query, so never run it on
a mutation outside a rollback-able transaction. Buffers reveal disk versus cache, and `loops` times rows
reveals a nested-loop blow-up.

---

## Reliability, testing, and operations

**37. 🟡** What must `/healthz` and `/readyz` do differently?
`/healthz` is liveness: is the process alive? It must **not** check dependencies, or a database blip
restarts every pod at once and turns a blip into an outage. `/readyz` is readiness: can this instance
serve traffic? It checks dependencies, so a degraded database removes the pod from the load balancer
without killing it.

**38. 🔴** Why does layer order in a Dockerfile matter to the build cache?
Each layer is a diff of the previous filesystem. Copy the lockfile and install before copying source,
and the dependency layer is cached for every commit that does not change dependencies. Reverse the
order and you reinstall on every code change.

**39. 🟡** What is the difference between a flaky test and a missing test?
A flaky test teaches you to ignore red, which is strictly worse than no test because it erodes the
signal for the whole suite. Causes: real timing dependencies, shared state between tests, ordering
assumptions, reliance on the network or the clock. Fix the cause, quarantine with an owner and a
deadline, and never simply re-run in CI.

**40. 🔴** What is an error budget, and how does it change what you ship?
The allowed unreliability: `(1 − SLO) × period`. 99.9% over 30 days is about 43 minutes. With budget
left, you ship faster and take more risk; with it spent, you stop feature work and fix reliability.
The point is making the trade-off explicit, so reliability stops losing every argument by default.

---

## Bonus 15 — mixed, for a final drill

**B1. 🟢** Cookie versus `localStorage` for an auth token?
A cookie is sent automatically and can be `HttpOnly` (invisible to JavaScript), `Secure`, and
`SameSite`, so it is protected from the most common theft path. `localStorage` is readable by any
script on the page, so one XSS exfiltrates the token. Cookies have a small size limit and ride along
on every matching request.

**B2. 🟢** `401` versus `403` in code, and why the logging distinction matters?
`401` means "authenticate" and should include `WWW-Authenticate`; `403` means "not allowed". Log them
differently: a 401 spike usually means expired credentials or a broken client, while a 403 spike
usually means a permissions bug or an attack.

**B3. 🟡** What is idempotent about HTTP `GET`, and why is that not a guarantee about your API?
The specification requires GET to be safe — no side effects — which makes it idempotent in theory.
But a badly built endpoint increments a counter in a GET handler. The spec constraint is on server
behaviour, and only holds if you honour it.

**B4. 🟡** N+1 in one sentence, and one fix.
One logical operation issues one query per result row; fix with an eager join or a batched `IN`
query.

**B5. 🟡** What does a database constraint buy you that application validation does not?
Enforcement under concurrency and across every writer, including a buggy script and a manual `psql`
session. Validation in application code is advisory; `UNIQUE` is not.

**B6. 🟡** What is a race condition, and the general fix?
Two operations interleave so the outcome depends on timing. The general fix is a lock, a unique
constraint, or a single atomic statement — not application-level check-then-act.

**B7. 🟡** What does `500` versus `503` tell an operator?
`503` is "temporarily unavailable, retry with backoff" and should carry `Retry-After`. `500` is "we
have a bug". Telling a client to retry a 500 is usually wrong; retrying a 503 is usually right.

**B8. 🔴** What is cache stampede, and how do you prevent it?
Many requests for one key miss together, the origin is hammered, and it falls over. Prevent with
request coalescing (one refresh, everyone waits), a short stale-while-revalidate window, jittered
TTLs, and a lock on the miss path.

**B9. 🔴** What is a thundering herd, and where else does it appear?
The same problem elsewhere: cache expiry, a service restart clearing all connections at once, a token
expiring for all clients simultaneously, or a scheduled job running on every instance. Fixes: jitter,
coordination, and graceful drain.

**B10. 🟡** What is a connection pool, and why does exhaustion cascade?
A bounded set of reusable database connections. A slow query holds a connection, so concurrency rises,
the queue grows, latency rises, and more queries hold connections longer. Bound the pool, set a short
acquisition timeout so requests fail fast rather than queue, and fix the slow query.

**B11. 🔴** What does eventual consistency mean from the user's perspective, and what is the
alternative?
The write is not visible everywhere immediately, so a user who writes and immediately reads a
different node sees stale data. Alternatives: read your own writes from the primary, use a
read-your-writes session token, or accept staleness and design the UI not to contradict itself — do
not show a modal that a background refresh immediately contradicts.

**B12. 🟡** `EXCEPT` versus `INTERSECT`, and when do you use them?
Set operators on compatible result sets: `UNION`, `UNION ALL` (keeps duplicates, often much faster),
`INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT`. Use `EXCEPT` for a set-difference anti-join; `NOT IN` with a nullable column is a
trap, because one `NULL` makes the whole predicate unknown.

**B13. 🔴** What is a saga, and how does it differ from a distributed transaction?
A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions, so no global lock or two-phase commit is
needed. Each step has a rollback. The trade-off is no isolation — intermediate states are visible — so
you need idempotency, a reliable compensator, and a way to resume from a crash mid-saga.

**B14. ⚫** What is a CRDT, and when is it worth the complexity?
A data structure whose merges are commutative, associative, and idempotent, so replicas converge
without coordination. Worth it for genuinely collaborative editing, counters, and sets. Not worth it
for most products: large complexity, larger payloads, subtle semantics, and it does not solve intent —
two users deleting the same text is still a product decision.

**B15. 🔴** What is backpressure, and name three places it appears?
Resisting overload by making the queue upstream finite and slowing producers. It appears in a bounded
queue between services, a `bufferedAmount` threshold on a WebSocket, and a connection pool with a short
acquisition timeout. Without it, latency grows until everything times out and the failure moves from
slow to broken.

---

## Scoring yourself

| Score | Meaning | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2, under 30s | Ready | Move on |
| 1, correct but slow | Known, not owned | Rehearse once more; it comes fast under pressure |
| 0 or hedged | Not known | Re-teach, then return tomorrow |
| Confident and wrong | Worst case | Trace the specific fact; do not re-read the whole topic |

Run the set twice. The gap between the two runs is your real learning rate. If it is small, you are
done with this set; if it is large, keep going.

---

practice.reference:
One gate for the whole roadmap, top to bottom. Every box must be genuinely ticked — "mostly" is
unticked. Score the ticks: **0–35** not ready, start at X.2.4 or X.2.1; **36–60** ready for a junior
loop with gaps you can talk about; **61–80** ready for a solid mid loop; **81–100** ready for
mid/senior loops, where the remaining work is depth and interview polish.

---

## 1. Foundations you cannot be interviewed on

- [ ] I can explain the event loop, microtasks versus macrotasks, and where promises land.
- [ ] I know what `typeof null` returns and why.
- [ ] I can explain closures and name a bug they cause.
- [ ] I understand `this` in methods, arrow functions, and callbacks.
- [ ] I can say what hoisting is and what the temporal dead zone is.
- [ ] I can explain shallow versus deep copy, and when a spread is a bug.
- [ ] I know `unknown` over `any`, and what `readonly` does not guarantee.
- [ ] I can explain what a discriminated union buys and how `never` works in a switch.
- [ ] I know the box model, `box-sizing`, and why they cause bugs.
- [ ] I can choose between grid and flexbox and explain why.
- [ ] I know what causes layout shift and how to prevent it.
- [ ] I can honour `prefers-reduced-motion` and `prefers-color-scheme`.
- [ ] I can explain `localStorage`, cookies, `sessionStorage`, and IndexedDB trade-offs.
- [ ] I can explain what a CSP actually stops.

## 2. HTTP and API design

- [ ] I can walk the journey from typing a URL to first paint, in order.
- [ ] I know `401` versus `403` versus `404`, including the security reasoning for `404`.
- [ ] I can explain a conditional request with `ETag` and `If-None-Match` end to end.
- [ ] I know what `Cache-Control: no-store` is for and when I need it.
- [ ] I can explain `Vary` and one bug it prevents.
- [ ] I can explain the CORS preflight, when it happens, and what it does not stop.
- [ ] I know `PUT` versus `PATCH` and the idempotency requirement of each.
- [ ] I can define idempotency and name where it must hold in my system.
- [ ] I know what belongs in a `429` response.
- [ ] I can explain when `OFFSET` pagination is wrong and what replaces it.
- [ ] I can describe versioning an API without breaking clients.
- [ ] I can write one error contract (problem details) used everywhere.

## 3. Data

- [ ] I can read `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` and know what estimated-versus-actual means.
- [ ] I can give five reasons an index is not used, with a real example.
- [ ] I understand composite index column order and its interaction with `WHERE`/`ORDER BY`.
- [ ] I can diagnose and fix an N+1, and I have a test that catches one.
- [ ] I can explain each isolation level and the concrete anomaly it permits.
- [ ] I can explain a partial index and when it beats a full one.
- [ ] I can design a schema that makes invalid states impossible.
- [ ] I know when a unique constraint beats application validation, and why.
- [ ] I can implement keyset pagination with a signed cursor.
- [ ] I can explain connection pooling and how exhaustion cascades.

## 4. Reliability and operations

- [ ] I can explain timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and what each stops.
- [ ] I can write a retry policy with backoff, full jitter, a cap, and a budget.
- [ ] I know what idempotent consumer design is and where the record must live.
- [ ] I can run a schema migration with no downtime via expand/contract.
- [ ] I can distinguish `/healthz` from `/readyz` and explain the failure mode of confusing them.
- [ ] I can implement graceful shutdown and explain what happens without it during a deploy.
- [ ] I can debug a production issue with only logs, and know what logs cannot tell me.
- [ ] I can describe a real incident with a timeline and a preventive change.
- [ ] I can build a multi-stage Dockerfile, non-root, digest-pinned.
- [ ] I can write CI with parallel gates, concurrency groups, and coverage thresholds.
- [ ] I can rehearse a rollback and describe the trigger that would make me do it.
- [ ] I know which metrics are correct and that labels must not include user or URL.

## 5. Frontend depth (skip if backend-leaning; invert section 6)

- [ ] I can say precisely why a component re-rendered.
- [ ] I know what `useEffect` compares, and can name the stale-closure trap.
- [ ] I understand keys and what an array index breaks.
- [ ] I know when `useMemo` and `useCallback` are a pessimisation.
- [ ] I can separate server state from client state and say why duplicating causes bugs.
- [ ] I can implement optimistic updates and handle every failure case.
- [ ] I can build a form with schema-driven validation and the server as authority.
- [ ] I can prevent a double submit, and know why disabling the button is not enough.
- [ ] I can explain hydration mismatch: cause, symptom, three fixes.
- [ ] I know what an error boundary cannot catch.
- [ ] I have shipped a keyboard-complete, axe-clean feature.
- [ ] I have profiled a real app and fixed something because of the profile.
- [ ] I can name my JavaScript budget and what I would remove from it.

## 6. Backend and system design depth (skip if frontend-leaning)

- [ ] I can design a rate limiter and say what happens when its state store is down.
- [ ] I can design a read-heavy and a write-heavy system, and name the differentiator.
- [ ] I can explain fan-out on read versus write, and where I would switch.
- [ ] I can explain queue delivery guarantees and what a DLQ is for.
- [ ] I know how replication lag affects read-after-write and how I would preserve it.
- [ ] I can pick a shard key and say what happens during a rebalance.
- [ ] I can name the three multi-tenancy models and their costs.
- [ ] I can design a read path with a cache and explain the invalidation.
- [ ] I can reason about consistency, availability, and perceived staleness.
- [ ] I can size a system: DAU, requests/second, storage, and what dominates cost.
- [ ] I can model data with real constraints and say what each prevents.
- [ ] I can implement token rotation with reuse detection and say which attack it catches.

## 7. Security

- [ ] I know why a password is hashed with a memory-hard function and never encrypted.
- [ ] I can explain CSRF and two defences, and know CORS is not one.
- [ ] I can prevent SQL injection, including dynamic identifiers and sort columns.
- [ ] I can prevent XSS: escaping, allowlist sanitisation, and CSP as the backstop.
- [ ] I can explain SSRF and how to prevent it.
- [ ] I know how to store secrets and can prove one is not in an image.
- [ ] I can prevent IDOR, and know hiding an id is not a defence.
- [ ] I know what I would do on the first day after a credential leak.
- [ ] I have a threat model for at least one project.

## 8. Projects and evidence

- [ ] One project is deployed at a real URL anyone can open.
- [ ] It has a README with architecture, a decision log, and "what I would change".
- [ ] It has tests that would catch my next bug, with honestly explainable coverage.
- [ ] It has a dashboard, or structured logs plus error tracking.
- [ ] I can answer, for three decisions: why this, what it cost, what would change my mind.
- [ ] I can name the weakest part and the first thing I would do about it.
- [ ] I know which part breaks first at 10× traffic, and how I would find out.
- [ ] I have a 90-second pitch and it is exactly 90 seconds.

## 9. Interview mechanics

- [ ] I have a written 90-second project pitch, rehearsed to time.
- [ ] I have six STAR stories: conflict, failure, ambiguity, feedback, impact, disagreement.
- [ ] I can answer "your weakest decision" with a specific regret and a fix.
- [ ] I can answer "how do you know it worked" with a metric, not an opinion.
- [ ] I can ask six good questions about the team, the work, and the failure modes.
- [ ] I have rehearsed a 45-minute design and a 30-minute coding problem out loud.
- [ ] Screen sharing, audio, camera, and backup connection are verified.
- [ ] I have read the job post and can name three nouns from it to use in conversation.

## 10. Discipline

- [ ] I have a weekly schedule with fixed anchors sustainable for 24 weeks.
- [ ] I have a Sunday review that re-plans the coming week.
- [ ] My X.2.5 diagnostic is scored and I know my two weakest sections.
- [ ] I have a written plan per gap, with the artifact that closes it.
- [ ] I have booked mock interviews in advance.
- [ ] I have told one person my schedule, so someone notices if I stop.

---

## The three questions that decide everything

If you can answer these well, tick the rest approximately. If you cannot, ticking the rest is
self-deception.

**1. Can you tell me about a hard technical problem, including what you got wrong first?**
The test is whether there is a wrong turn. A story with no wrong turn is either untrue or a project
summary in disguise.

**2. Tell me about a decision you made that other people disagreed with.**
The test is whether you named a constraint rather than a preference, said what it cost, and can say
what would change your mind.

**3. How do you know whether it is working?**
The test is whether you name a metric, a baseline, and a threshold — and whether you have been the
person who changed something because of a number.

---

## The last honest warnings

- **Ticking boxes is not readiness.** Readiness is an unexpected follow-up where you must build the
  answer live. Practise that, not the list.
- **A gap you can name is survivable.** A gap you cannot name is fatal, because the first probe finds
  it and then everything else you said is discounted.
- **Do not fake seniority.** Interviewed at the wrong level you lose on depth you do not have and
  look like you are bluffing. Interviewed at the right level you win on trajectory, which is what they
  can actually assess.
- **The plan that survives is the one you are still doing in week 14.** Choose the plan whose weekday
  block you can protect tonight, not the most ambitious-looking one.
- **Anyone can learn this.** The people who get hired are the ones still working on it after the
  third month, when it stopped being fun. That is the entire differentiator.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Why this project, and what it proves**

The smallest project that still exercises the whole browser rendering pipeline, and the one place
you have no excuse for hiding behind a framework. It proves you can write semantic HTML that
survives a validator and a screen reader; that you understand the box model, cascade, specificity,
and inheritance well enough to debug a layout without `!important`; that you can build responsive
layouts with fluid units instead of magic pixel breakpoints; and that you can ship — DNS, TLS,
env config, cache headers, a build step, a lighthouse score you can defend.

The interview story is unusually strong because it is verifiable. "My site scores 100 on
accessibility and performance" is checkable in thirty seconds, so this project returns more per
hour invested than any other on this list.

**Requirements**

*Must-have*

- 🟢 Semantic HTML5: `header`/`nav`/`main`/`section`/`article`/`footer`, one `h1`, no heading
  skips, `alt` on every meaningful image, a skip-to-content link.
- 🟢 Hand-written responsive layout: custom properties as a design token layer, `clamp()` for
  fluid type, grid and flexbox for structure, no fixed heights on text containers, media queries
  only where genuinely needed.
- 🟢 Dark/light themes via `prefers-color-scheme` plus a manual toggle persisted to
  `localStorage`, with all animation gated on `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- 🟢 Vanilla JS modules rendering three views from a data file: a project grid, a filter/search
  control, and a detail view. No framework.
- 🟢 Progressive enhancement — all projects, text, and contact links present in the HTML source,
  not injected by JavaScript.
- 🟢 Contact form validating on the client and posting to a real endpoint, with real loading,
  success, and error states.
- 🟢 Tooling and delivery: Vite, ESLint + Prettier, deployed to Netlify/Vercel/GitHub Pages or
  S3 + CloudFront with a real certificate.
- 🟢 Lighthouse 100/100/100/100 on the deployed URL, mobile-throttled.
- 🟢 `README.md` with the decision log, a live URL, and a screenshot.

*Stretch*

- 🟡 Static content pipeline: Markdown with front matter compiled to JSON at build time, so adding
  a project means adding a file.
- 🟡 Security headers in the host config: CSP, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`,
  `Permissions-Policy`.
- 🟡 Per-project real URLs via the History API, linkable and back-button correct.
- 🟡 `IntersectionObserver` reveal animations, disabled entirely under reduced motion.
- 🟡 Build-time Open Graph images, `sitemap.xml`, canonical URLs.
- 🔴 Hand-rolled fuzzy search over project metadata with a debounced, keyboard-navigable UI.

**Architecture**

- `index.html` — the semantic shell, containing the full static content fallback.
- `main.js` — entry module: imports views, wires the router, boots the theme.
- `data/projects.js` — the single source of truth: `slug`, `title`, `stack[]`, `year`, `summary`,
  `highlights[]`, `links`, `tags[]`.
- `views/grid.js` — renders the grid with `document.createElement`, never `innerHTML` with
  interpolated data.
- `views/detail.js` — one project by slug, updating `document.title` and the meta description.
- `lib/router.js` — ~40-line History API router: route table, `popstate`, a click interceptor
  that respects modifier keys and `target=_blank`, and focus management after navigation.
- `lib/theme.js` — `localStorage` → `matchMedia` fallback → sets `data-theme` on `<html>` before
  first paint via a sub-400-byte inline script.
- `lib/store.js` — ~30-line observable store (`subscribe`, `set`, immutable updates) used by the
  filter UI and the theme.
- `lib/dom.js` — the five functions you need: `el()`, `frag()`, `clear()`, `mount()`.
- `styles/{tokens,layout,components,utilities}.css` — tokens, structure, components, and only
  four utility classes.

Data model (JSDoc-typed so editors check it without a build step):

```js
/**
 * @typedef {Object} Project
 * @property {string} slug    kebab-case, unique, the route key
 * @property {string} title
 * @property {string} year
 * @property {string[]} stack  ordered most-important-first; first 3 render as chips
 * @property {string} summary  one sentence, max 140 chars, reused in meta description
 * @property {string[]} highlights  3 bullets, each starting with a verb
 * @property {{live?: string, repo?: string, writeup?: string}} links
 * @property {string[]} tags  used by the filter UI
 */
```

Request paths (static, so "request paths" means navigation and asset delivery):

1. **Cold load**: HTML (revalidated, `max-age=0, must-revalidate`) → CSS (immutable, hashed) → JS
   bundle (immutable, hashed) → font (subset, preloaded, `font-display: swap`). Critical CSS inlined
   under 14 KB. Nothing third-party in the critical path.
2. **Project detail**: `/projects/atlas-chat` → edge serves `index.html` via SPA rewrite → JS
   hydrates the route and updates title and meta. Accept the SEO limitation knowingly, or add a
   build-time static copy of each project's meta.
3. **Form submit**: `POST /api/contact` → rate limit → honeypot → serverless function →
   transactional email → 202 with a request id. Never echo the submitted address into the DOM
   unescaped.

**The hard parts**

1. **A 100 Performance score on mobile throttle.** Reserve every image's aspect ratio (`width` and
   `height` attributes), serve modern formats, inline critical CSS so first render does not wait on
   a stylesheet, and — the detail people miss — use a metric-adjusted fallback font:
   `@font-face { font-family: Fallback; src: local(...); size-adjust: 97%; ascent-override: ... }`
   with `font-display: swap`, so the swap does not shift layout. Then delete code; bundle analysis
   usually finds 30% you do not ship.
2. **A theme toggle that does not flash white at 2am.** A sub-400-byte inline script in `<head>`
   reads `localStorage`, falls back to `matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)')`, and sets
   `document.documentElement.dataset.theme` before the body parses. Every colour is a custom
   property redefined inside `[data-theme='dark']`; no component rule ever hardcodes a hex value.
3. **Rendering without a flash of empty content.** Build-time static markup for the default view,
   then adopt the existing DOM on boot rather than clearing it — hydrate by walking `[data-render]`
   markers. Avoid `opacity: 0` + `visibility: hidden` for the pre-hydration state; it breaks
   no-JS and confuses assistive tech. Use `content-visibility: auto` with `contain-intrinsic-size`
   for offscreen sections instead.
4. **A filter UI that stays at 60fps with 200 items.** Keep a `Map<slug, HTMLElement>` of rendered
   nodes and toggle a class or `hidden` instead of re-rendering; wrap card text in
   `content-visibility: auto`; debounce input at 120ms on the trailing edge; coalesce rapid changes
   into one `requestAnimationFrame` pass.
5. **A modal that is actually accessible.** Trap focus with `inert` on the rest of the tree,
   handle `Escape`, restore focus to the trigger on close, `role="dialog"` with `aria-modal` and a
   labelled title, and lock scroll without layout shift by setting `overflow: hidden` on
   `documentElement` and compensating with `padding-right: var(--scrollbar-width)`. All six details
   get probed.

**Milestones**

| # | Task | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| M1 | Scaffold + design tokens (colour, type, spacing, radii via `clamp()`) | 4h |
| M2 | Static semantic shell: all sections in HTML, validator clean | 4h |
| M3 | Responsive layout: header, about, grid, contact, footer, 320→2560 | 6h |
| M4 | Theming and motion: no-flash inline script, toggle, reduced motion | 3h |
| M5 | Data-driven grid + real detail routes from `data/projects.js` | 5h |
| M6 | Filtering and search: tag filter, text search, debounced, node reuse | 4h |
| M7 | Contact form: validation, POST, loading/success/error, honeypot | 3h |
| M8 | Accessibility pass: axe clean, full keyboard walkthrough, contrast | 4h |
| M9 | Performance pass: critical CSS, fonts, images, cache headers, Lighthouse | 4h |
| M10 | Deploy, security headers via `curl -I`, README + decision log | 3h |
| S | Stretch: Markdown pipeline, static meta, JSON resume export | 6h |

~44h core, ~6h stretch. At 8h/week, six weeks.

**Evaluation rubric**

0–3 per row, 30 total. Below 20: keep fixing. 26–30: genuinely competitive for any
frontend-leaning junior screen.

| Dimension | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Semantic HTML / a11y | div soup | landmarks, wrong headings | semantic and ordered, alt text | axe clean, keyboard complete, screen reader verified |
| CSS architecture | inline styles, `!important` | works, duplication | tokens, no magic numbers | tokens + primitives, zero leakage between components |
| Responsive craft | fixed px, breaks | media queries work | fluid units, clean 320→2560 | content-driven breakpoints, no scroll at any width |
| JS architecture | inline handlers, globals | one big file | ES modules, small functions, explicit state | store + router + views, no globals, tree-shaken |
| Performance | slow | assets unoptimised | hashed assets, lazy images | Lighthouse 100 mobile, inlined critical CSS, metric-adjusted fonts |
| Deployment & ops | localhost | deploy button | domain, HTTPS, headers | headers in config, CI deploy on push, decision log committed |

**What an interviewer probes**

- "Walk me through the critical rendering path" — expect HTML → render-blocking CSS → parser-
  blocking JS → first paint → lazy, and what you inlined and why.
- "How did you avoid a theme flash?" This separates people who shipped from people who copied.
- "Why `clamp()` over media queries?" Expect content-driven scaling, fewer breakpoints, no
  device-specific guessing.
- "How do you know it's accessible?" Automated tooling finds roughly a third of issues; the rest is
  a manual keyboard pass. An automated score alone is a warning sign.
- "What is your JS payload and what would you remove?" Expect a number in KB and at least one
  deletion candidate.

**Follow-on extension**

Build-time content pipeline so case studies are files; per-route analytics with one number and one
decision per page; `robots.txt`, `sitemap.xml`, canonicals, build-time OG images; a global error
listener swapping in a friendly message; documented cache headers with versioned assets and an
invalidation story; and a service worker only if you can state precisely what it buys a portfolio
(precached shell, network-first documents) — otherwise a deliberate omission is the better answer.

keyConcepts: Why this project, and what it proves

🟢 Create, inline edit, complete, delete, due date, priority, notes, filter, sort, search, and
🟢 localStorage persistence with a versioned schema ({ version: 3, tasks: [...] }) and one
🟢 A pure (state, action) => state reducer with no side effects and no Date.now() inside;
🟢 Undo as an inverse action log, not state snapshots.
🟢 Keyboard: n new, / search, j/k navigate, e edit, x toggle, Enter save,
🟢 Tests, in Vitest plus Playwright:
🟢 Honest coverage — 90%+ on the domain layer, with an explanation of what the uncovered lines are.
🟡 Accessibility: a real listbox pattern with aria-selected, live-region announcements for
🟡 A deployed preview so a reviewer can run it.

**Why this project, and what it proves**

This is where most candidates claim competence and cannot demonstrate it. A to-do app looks
trivial until you require typed domain models, a state machine for task lifecycle, an audit trail of
transitions, and a test suite proving the reducer correct. It proves you use TypeScript as a design
tool — expressing the domain as discriminated unions and total functions so the compiler finds your
bugs; that you understand the unit/integration/e2e split and can write tests that fail for real
reasons rather than implementation details; that you can model stateful UI without a framework; and
that you can persist, migrate, and reason about failure.

The interview story is about *decisions*: why a union over five booleans, why one reducer, why the
tests test behaviour rather than markup.

**Requirements**

*Must-have*

- 🟢 `strict` mode plus `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`,
  `noImplicitOverride`. Zero `any`; `@ts-expect-error` only with a comment saying why the compiler
  is wrong.
- 🟢 A domain model that cannot be invalid: status as a discriminated union, not five booleans.
- 🟢 Create, inline edit, complete, delete, due date, priority, notes, filter, sort, search, and
  undo of the last destructive action.
- 🟢 `localStorage` persistence with a versioned schema (`{ version: 3, tasks: [...] }`) and one
  migration function per version.
- 🟢 A pure `(state, action) => state` reducer with no side effects and no `Date.now()` inside;
  time and randomness injected.
- 🟢 Undo as an inverse action log, not state snapshots.
- 🟢 Keyboard: `n` new, `/` search, `j`/`k` navigate, `e` edit, `x` toggle, `Enter` save,
  `Escape` cancel, `?` shortcut overlay.
- 🟢 Tests, in Vitest plus Playwright:
  - Unit: the full transition table, including invalid transitions.
  - Property-based, with `fast-check`: random action sequences asserting purity (deep-frozen
    input), no task lost, and undo restoring the exact prior state.
  - Integration: the repository against a real in-memory or mocked store, including v1 migration.
  - E2E: create-and-complete, filter-and-search, migrate-an-old-payload.
- 🟢 Honest coverage — 90%+ on the domain layer, with an explanation of what the uncovered lines are.
- 🟡 Accessibility: a real listbox pattern with `aria-selected`, live-region announcements for
  filter results and undo, full keyboard operation.
- 🟡 A deployed preview so a reviewer can run it.

*Stretch*

- 🟡 Offline-first: an IndexedDB outbox with idempotent replay and per-field last-write-wins
  conflict resolution keyed on `updatedAt` + `deviceId`.
- 🟡 Recurrence rules via `rrule`, expanded lazily over a 90-day horizon.
- 🟡 A hand-written windowing virtualiser for 10k tasks.
- 🔴 A time-travel debugger: a ring buffer of every action and resulting state with a scrubber.
- 🔴 `tsc --noEmit` in CI plus `eslint-plugin-typed-linting` and a type-coverage gate.
- ⚫ Property tests generating whole task graphs, not just action sequences.

**Architecture**

React + TypeScript, chosen because the reducer/selector split tests cleanly and the story is about
types rather than a framework.

- `src/domain/task.ts` — types only. No imports, no runtime logic beyond constructors.
- `src/domain/reducer.ts` — the pure reducer.
- `src/domain/selectors.ts` — memoised derived data: filter → sort → search.
- `src/domain/invariants.ts` — `assertInvariants(state)` used in dev mode and in tests.
- `src/data/repository.ts` / `localRepo.ts` / `indexedDbRepo.ts` — the persistence interface and
  two implementations.
- `src/state/AppContext.tsx` — provider wiring `useReducer` plus the undo log.
- `src/components/{TaskList,TaskRow,TaskEditor,FilterBar,SearchInput,ShortcutOverlay,UndoToast}.tsx`
- `src/test/` — co-located; no network to mock, so no `msw`.

Data model:

```ts
type TaskStatus = 'active' | 'completed' | 'archived';
type Priority = 'low' | 'normal' | 'high';

interface BaseTask {
  readonly id: TaskId;          // branded: string & { readonly __brand: 'TaskId' }
  readonly createdAt: number;   // epoch ms, injected
  readonly updatedAt: number;
  readonly revision: number;    // bumped per mutation, for optimistic concurrency
}
interface ActiveTask    extends BaseTask { status: 'active'; title: string; priority: Priority;
                                          dueAt: number | null; tags: readonly string[]; notes: string }
interface CompletedTask extends ActiveTask { status: 'completed'; completedAt: number }
interface ArchivedTask  extends BaseTask  { status: 'archived'; title: string; archivedAt: number;
                                          archivedFrom: 'completed' | 'active' }
type Task = ActiveTask | CompletedTask | ArchivedTask;

interface AppState {
  readonly tasks: readonly Task[];
  readonly filter: Filter;
  readonly query: string;
  readonly selection: readonly TaskId[];
  readonly undoStack: readonly UndoEntry[];
  readonly schemaVersion: number;
}

type Action =
  | { type: 'task/created';   payload: ActiveTask }
  | { type: 'task/completed'; payload: { id: TaskId; at: number } }
  | { type: 'task/reopened';  payload: { id: TaskId; at: number } }
  | { type: 'task/archived';  payload: { id: TaskId; at: number } }
  | { type: 'task/edited';    payload: { id: TaskId; patch: EditablePatch; at: number } }
  | { type: 'task/deleted';   payload: { id: TaskId; removed: Task } }
  | { type: 'task/restored';  payload: Task }
  | { type: 'filter/changed'; payload: Partial<Filter> }
  | { type: 'query/changed';  payload: string }
  | { type: 'selection/toggled'; payload: TaskId };
```

The union's payoff: `task/completed` only type-checks when the task is not already completed,
enforced at the reducer boundary, and a `switch` that misses a variant becomes a compile error via
`assertNever`.

Request paths (local-first, so these are read paths):

1. **Boot**: `getItem('tasks:v3')` → `JSON.parse` inside `try` → `migrate(raw, 3)` → reducer init
   → render. Parse or migration failure falls back to `[]` with a non-blocking banner, never a
   blank screen.
2. **Write**: dispatch → reducer → a `useEffect` on the tasks slice debounced 250ms →
   `repository.save`. Without the debounce, keystroke-rate edits serialise forty writes a second.
3. **Undo**: pop the last `UndoEntry` (the inverse action plus any removed task) and dispatch it.
   Memory is O(actions), not O(state size).
4. **Read model**: `selectVisibleTasks(state)` memoised on `(tasks, filter, query)` so selection
   changes do not re-run filtering.

**The hard parts**

1. **Making illegal states unrepresentable.** Discriminated union plus narrowing at the reducer
   boundary: each case asserts the current status, and the switch ends with
   `default: return assertNever(action)` where `assertNever` takes `never` and returns `never`.
   Add `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch` and `noImplicitReturns`. Adding a status field becomes a compile
   error everywhere it must be handled.
2. **A test suite that catches regressions rather than inflating a number.** Generate the reducer
   transition table over every `(status, action)` pair and assert the resulting status, the
   `revision`, and that untouched tasks are reference-equal — which catches accidental copies.
   Then `fast-check` properties: purity (`reduce(s, a)` twice deep-equals and never mutates a
   deep-frozen `s`), no loss (every id present before is present after, modulo explicit deletes),
   and undo fidelity (`undo(apply(s, a))` deep-equals `s`). Property tests find the bug you did not
   think of; that is the entire point.
3. **Migrations that never brick a returning user.** Store `{ version, data }` with pure
   `migrate1to2`, `migrate2to3`, reduced by a `migrate(raw)` dispatcher. Test each step with a
   fixture captured from the real old build, plus an e2e test that seeds v1 and asserts the user
   sees their tasks. Keep the original raw value until the new one is durably written, and wrap the
   write in `try` so a quota failure does not leave a half-migrated store.
4. **Undo without snapshots.** Each mutating action carries its inverse: `deleted` carries the
   removed `Task` so undo is a `restored` action; `edited` records the previous values of only the
   changed keys (diff the patch against current state); `completed` pairs with `reopened`. Cap at
   50 entries in a ring buffer. Have an answer ready for whether undo crosses filter changes — mine
   does, and it clears a filter that would hide the restored task, then announces it.
5. **Optimistic offline writes that converge.** A per-task `revision` checked on write; a pending
   queue in IndexedDB tagged with an `opId` so replay upserts by `opId` rather than appending; a
   conflict policy of last-write-wins *per field* with a recorded conflict log surfaced in a debug
   panel; and `online`/`offline` listeners to drain the queue. The detail that earns credit:
   per-field LWW, so a title edit on one device does not clobber a tag edit on another.

**Milestones**

| # | Task | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| M1 | Types and invariants: union, branded `TaskId`, `assertNever`, strict flags | 5h |
| M2 | Reducer complete: all actions, transitions, revision bumps | 6h |
| M3 | Property tests: purity, no-loss, undo fidelity, 1000 sequences | 5h |
| M4 | Persistence and migrations: repository interface, v1→v2→v3, failure fallback | 5h |
| M5 | UI: list, row, editor, filter, search, memoised selectors | 8h |
| M6 | Keyboard and a11y: shortcuts, focus management, live regions, listbox semantics | 5h |
| M7 | Undo/redo: inverse log, ring buffer, undo toast | 3h |
| M8 | E2E: Playwright config, three flows, CI on every push | 5h |
| M9 | Polish and deploy: error banner, empty states, perf, deploy | 4h |
| S | Stretch: IndexedDB outbox, time-travel debugger, virtualisation, recurrence | 8h |

~46h core, ~8h stretch.

**Evaluation rubric**

| Dimension | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TypeScript discipline | `any` everywhere | types in one file | discriminated unions, branded ids, `assertNever` | strict + `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, zero escapes, coverage gate |
| Domain modelling | booleans for status | optionals everywhere | union makes illegal states unrepresentable | plus invariants asserted in dev and tests |
| Reducer & state | scattered `setState` | one mutating reducer | pure reducer, injected time, memoised selectors | plus an action log enabling time travel |
| Tests | happy path only | some unit | unit + integration + property + e2e | properties that would have caught a real bug; coverage explained |
| Persistence | single blob | load and save | versioned schema, migrations, failure fallback | idempotent offline outbox with a conflict log |
| UX & a11y | mouse only | labels only | full keyboard, live regions, focus management | discoverable shortcut system, undo that respects the view |

**What an interviewer probes**

- "Why a union and not booleans?" Expect: illegal combinations become unrepresentable.
- "Show me a bug your property test found." Have a real answer; if you have never run them, say so
  and describe what you would assert.
- "How would you test undo?" Expect: inverse actions, not snapshots, plus a fidelity property.
- "What happens when the schema changes?" Expect: versioned payload, per-version pure migrations,
  fixtures from real old payloads.
- "How would this scale to 100k tasks?" Expect: virtualisation, and honest naming of what breaks
  first (recomputation per keystroke in search, then DOM count).

**Follow-on extension**

A real HTTP backend behind the same repository interface (`HttpRepo`) with optimistic UI and
rollback; request deduplication and a retry queue; an outbox with idempotency keys; sanitised error
reporting via an error boundary; OpenTelemetry spans around repository calls; a feature flag so the
time-travel debugger loads only when enabled; and a migration documented as reversible or explicitly
irreversible.

topics.referenceMarkdown: **Why this project, and what it proves** This is where "I have done a tutorial" ends. Prove it: submit `'; drop table users; --` and assert a 200 with escaped output, not a 500. topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Why this project, and what it proves**

Payments turn vague answers into obvious ones. Nearly everyone says "I built an e-commerce site";
almost none can explain idempotency keys, webhook ordering, authorize versus capture, why the client
must never set a price, or how to reconcile a ledger. It proves you can build a full Next.js app and
know what the framework does for you and what it does not (server components are not a transaction
boundary; `fetch` is not a transaction); that you integrate a payment processor correctly; that you
treat money as an append-only ledger in integer minor units; and that you can build the unglamorous
B2B surface — admin dashboard, bulk actions, CSV import/export, inventory adjustment with reason
codes, audit log.

**Requirements**

*Must-have*

- 🟢 Next.js 15 App Router + TypeScript, Tailwind, Prisma with PostgreSQL, Stripe Checkout plus
  webhooks, Zod, Auth.js or your own session cookies, Vitest + Playwright.
- 🟢 Catalog: products with variants, price in integer minor units plus a currency column, images,
  per-variant inventory with a non-negative constraint, categories, search.
- 🟢 Server-side cart keyed to a session cookie so it survives a device change; add, remove, quantity
  updates clamped to available stock with a clear message when stock moves.
- 🟢 Checkout: a Checkout Session created server-side from re-read prices, with the cart frozen into
  an `orders` row in `pending` before the redirect, plus an idempotency key derived from the cart
  version so a double click creates one order.
- 🟢 Webhooks: `checkout.session.completed`, `payment_intent.succeeded`,
  `payment_intent.payment_failed`, `charge.refunded`, `charge.dispute.created`. Signature verified
  against the raw body; events persisted to `webhook_events` keyed by `event.id` for idempotent
  replay; handlers order-insensitive because they read current state.
- 🟢 Order lifecycle `pending → paid → fulfilled | cancelled`, plus `refunded` and
  `partially_refunded`; money movements in append-only `ledger_entries`.
- 🟢 Admin dashboard: product CRUD, inventory adjustment with a reason code and an audit entry,
  order list with filters, order detail with a timeline, refund action, CSV export.
- 🟡 Inventory correctness: decrement inside the transaction that marks the order paid, with
  `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` or an atomic `UPDATE … WHERE stock >= n` and a check on rows affected. Never
  decrement on add-to-cart.
- 🟡 Emails queued through a worker, never inline.
- 🟢 Tests: webhooks replayed from fixtures including duplicates and out-of-order delivery; price
  tampering; oversell under concurrency; refund arithmetic; admin authz matrix.
- 🟡 Real Stripe CLI webhook forwarding in development, with a documented switch to production.

*Stretch*

- 🟡 Tax and shipping as a pluggable provider interface with a test double.
- 🟡 Multi-currency with an FX rate snapshot on the order, so historical totals never change.
- 🔴 A reconciliation job comparing Stripe balance transactions against internal entries, with drift
  alerting — the single most impressive item here.
- 🔴 Idempotent fulfillment as a saga: reserve stock → create shipment → notify, with compensating
  actions and a resumable state.
- 🔴 Dynamic variant combinations with a normalised `variants` table and a composite unique index on
  `(product_id, option1, option2)`.
- ⚫ Multi-vendor payouts with connected-account onboarding.

**Architecture**

- `src/app/(shop)/…` — server components for reads. `src/app/(admin)/…` — admin routes behind a
  layout guard *and* per-action authorization. `src/app/api/webhooks/stripe/route.ts` — reads the raw
  body (`await req.text()`), verifies with `stripe.webhooks.constructEvent(raw, sig, secret)`, then
  enqueues.
- `src/server/` — `db.ts`, `auth.ts`, `stripe.ts`,
  `services/{catalog,cart,checkout,orders,inventory,ledger,admin}.ts`, `jobs/queue.ts`,
  `jobs/handlers/*`.
- `src/server/money.ts` — the only module allowed to construct money values: `formatMinor`,
  `addMinor`, and `allocateProportional(totalMinor, weights)` with a largest-remainder correction so
  allocations sum exactly.
- `src/components/` — client components for cart interactions and admin forms, using transitions or
  `useOptimistic` where it helps.

Data model (abridged; constraints noted in comments):

```prisma
model Variant { id String @id @default(uuid()) productId String sku String @unique
  priceMinor Int  currency String @db.Char(3)  stock Int @default(0) }
// CHECK (stock >= 0) added with a raw migration

model Cart { id String @id @default(uuid()) sessionKey String @unique
  version Int @default(1)  items CartItem[] }

model Order { id String @id @default(uuid()) userId String?  sessionKey String
  status String @default("pending")
    // pending | paid | fulfilled | cancelled | refunded | partially_refunded | disputed
  currency String @db.Char(3)
  subtotalMinor Int  taxMinor Int  shippingMinor Int  totalMinor Int
  refundedMinor Int @default(0)
  stripeCheckoutSessionId String? @unique  stripePaymentIntentId String? @unique
  idempotencyKey String @unique  version Int @default(1)
  createdAt DateTime @default(now())  updatedAt DateTime @updatedAt
  @@index([userId, createdAt desc])  @@index([status, createdAt]) }

model OrderLine { id String @id @default(uuid()) orderId String  variantId String
  skuSnapshot String  titleSnapshot String
  unitPriceMinor Int  quantity Int  lineTotalMinor Int  taxMinor Int }
// snapshots, not joins: an invoice must not change when the catalog does

model LedgerEntry { id String @id @default(uuid()) orderId String
  kind String          // charge | refund | adjustment | payout | fee
  amountMinor Int      // signed: negative for money leaving you
  currency String @db.Char(3)  stripeRef String?
  metadata Json?  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
  @@index([orderId, createdAt]) }
// append-only; no updates, enforced by revoking UPDATE or a trigger

model WebhookEvent { id String @id   // stripe event id as primary key = idempotency
  type String  payload Json  receivedAt DateTime @default(now())
  processedAt DateTime?  attempts Int @default(0)  error String? }

model InventoryAdjustment { id String @id @default(uuid()) variantId String  sku String
  delta Int  reason String   // restock | return | damage | correction | manual
  orderId String?  actorId String  note String  createdAt DateTime @default(now()) }

model AuditLog { id String @id @default(uuid()) actorId String  action String
  entity String  entityId String  before Json  after Json
  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
  @@index([entity, entityId, createdAt desc]) }
```

Request paths:

1. **Add to cart** — `POST /api/cart/items` re-reads the price server-side from the DB, never from the
   body, upserts the line, clamps to stock, bumps `cart.version`, returns the cart. The body carries
   only `variantId` and `quantity`; that one rule kills price tampering.
2. **Checkout** — a transaction re-reads prices, verifies stock, computes tax and shipping through the
   provider interface, inserts the order `pending` with `idempotencyKey =
   sha256(sessionKey + cart.version)`, inserts `OrderLine` snapshots, then calls
   `stripe.checkout.sessions.create(params, { idempotencyKey })`, persists the session id, and returns
   the redirect URL. Two clicks produce the same key, so Stripe returns the same session.
3. **Webhook `checkout.session.completed`** — verify the signature on the raw body →
   `INSERT INTO webhook_events (id) … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` → 0 rows means already seen, return
   200 immediately → else enqueue. The handler, in a transaction: lock the order row; if already

**Why this project, and what it proves**

Payments turn vague answers into obvious ones. Nearly everyone says "I built an e-commerce site";
almost none can explain idempotency keys, webhook ordering, authorize versus capture, why the client

know what the framework does for you and what it does not (server components are not a transaction
boundary; `fetch` is not a transaction); that you integrate a payment processor correctly; that you
treat money as an append-only ledger in integer minor units; and that you can build the unglamorous

**Requirements**

*Must-have*

- 🟢 Next.js 15 App Router + TypeScript, Tailwind, Prisma with PostgreSQL, Stripe Checkout plus
  webhooks, Zod, Auth.js or your own session cookies, Vitest + Playwright.
- 🟢 Catalog: products with variants, price in integer minor units plus a currency column, images,
  per-variant inventory with a non-negative constraint, categories, search.
- 🟢 Server-side cart keyed to a session cookie so it survives a device change; add, remove, quantity
  updates clamped to available stock with a clear message when stock moves.
- 🟢 Checkout: a Checkout Session created server-side from re-read prices, with the cart frozen into
  an `orders` row in `pending` before the redirect, plus an idempotency key derived from the cart
  version so a double click creates one order.
- 🟢 Webhooks: `checkout.session.completed`, `payment_intent.succeeded`,
  `payment_intent.payment_failed`, `charge.refunded`, `charge.dispute.created`. Signature verified
  against the raw body; events persisted to `webhook_events` keyed by `event.id` for idempotent
  replay; handlers order-insensitive because they read current state.
- 🟢 Order lifecycle `pending → paid → fulfilled | cancelled`, plus `refunded` and
  `partially_refunded`; money movements in append-only `ledger_entries`.
- 🟢 Admin dashboard: product CRUD, inventory adjustment with a reason code and an audit entry,
  order list with filters, order detail with a timeline, refund action, CSV export.
- 🟡 Inventory correctness: decrement inside the transaction that marks the order paid, with
  `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` or an atomic `UPDATE … WHERE stock >= n` and a check on rows affected. Never
  decrement on add-to-cart.
- 🟡 Emails queued through a worker, never inline.
- 🟢 Tests: webhooks replayed from fixtures including duplicates and out-of-order delivery; price

- 🟡 Tax and shipping as a pluggable provider interface with a test double.
- 🟡 Multi-currency with an FX rate snapshot on the order, so historical totals never change.

  alerting — the single most impressive item here.
- 🔴 Idempotent fulfillment as a saga: reserve stock → create shipment → notify, with compensating
  actions and a resumable state.

model Cart { id String @id @default(uuid()) sessionKey String @unique
  version Int @default(1)  items CartItem[] }

model Order { id String @id @default(uuid()) userId String?  sessionKey String
  status String @default("pending")

  currency String @db.Char(3)
  subtotalMinor Int  taxMinor Int  shippingMinor Int  totalMinor Int
  refundedMinor Int @default(0)
  stripeCheckoutSessionId String? @unique  stripePaymentIntentId String? @unique
  idempotencyKey String @unique  version Int @default(1)
  createdAt DateTime @default(now())  updatedAt DateTime @updatedAt
  @@index([userId, createdAt desc])  @@index([status, createdAt]) }

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Why this project, and what it proves**

Real-time is where confident hand-waving shows. Almost everyone can say "use WebSockets"; far fewer
can explain the connection lifecycle, heartbeat and dead-peer detection, backpressure, at-most-once
versus at-least-once delivery, presence with expiring keys, and how the system behaves when an
instance dies with messages in flight. It proves you understand the handshake, auth, heartbeat,
close codes, and reconnect with backoff; that you understand horizontal scale, since one node is not a
system; that you can reason about delivery guarantees and per-conversation ordering; and that you can
observe a system whose failures are timing-dependent.

**Requirements**

*Must-have*

- 🟢 Node + TypeScript with `ws` (or Socket.IO if you want reconnection and rooms for free), Postgres
  for durable messages, Redis 7 for presence, fan-out, and rate limiting.
- 🟢 Authenticate during the handshake — verify a short-lived JWT before `upgrade`, and reject with
  the correct HTTP status. Never authenticate after accepting.
- 🟢 Conversations: 1:1 and group; a user joins only conversations they belong to; authorization
  checked on `join` and on every `send`.
- 🟢 Client-generated `clientMessageId` (UUID) with a unique constraint on
  `(conversationId, clientMessageId)`, so a retry never duplicates; the server assigns the
  authoritative id, `seq`, and `createdAt` and broadcasts the server record.
- 🟢 Ordering: a per-conversation gap-free sequence allocated under a row lock, with client-side gap
  detection and repair on reconnect.
- 🟢 Presence: online/offline/away with `presence:{userId}` and a ~45s TTL refreshed by the heartbeat,
  plus per-user active-conversation sets; multi-tab correct via a connection count and device id.
- 🟡 Typing indicators (ephemeral, never stored, dropped after 5s), read receipts, unread counts.
- 🟡 Reconnect with jittered exponential backoff, then `?after=<seq>` catch-up deduplicated by id.
- 🟢 Backpressure: a bounded per-connection queue with a slow-consumer policy — disconnect rather than
  let memory grow unboundedly.
- 🟢 Rate limiting per user and per connection in Redis with a sliding window.
- 🟢 Heartbeat: ping every 30s, terminate after two missed pongs (a 60s dead-peer window), close with a
  meaningful code.
- 🟢 Tests: unit for the message service and ordering; a two-instance integration test against one
  Redis; reconnect-and-catch-up; duplicate `clientMessageId`; slow consumer.
- 🟡 Client: conversation list, virtualised message list, infinite scroll, optimistic send with a
  pending state, connection status indicator.
- 🟡 Load test with `k6` or `autocannon`: 1,000 connections, a defined message rate, recorded p99
  broadcast latency.

*Stretch*

- 🟡 Multi-region: a presence directory recording each user's region so messages route to one region
  and skip cross-region fan-out for offline users.
- 🔴 End-to-end encryption with X25519 and `libsodium` sealed boxes, plus an explicit note that you
  must also solve key verification, and that the server can still be coerced to serve modified
  ciphertexts.
- 🔴 Delivery semantics (`sent`/`delivered`/`read`) in a separate table, never on the message.
- 🔴 Kafka replay with consumer offsets so a new instance rebuilds state.
- ⚫ Matrix-style federation.

**Architecture**

- `src/realtime/connectionRegistry.ts` — `connectionId → {userId, conversationIds, socket, queueDepth}`.
- `src/realtime/upgrade.ts` — handshake verification: parse cookies/headers, verify the JWT, check the
  session is unrevoked (Redis-cached), emit `401`/`403` and destroy the socket otherwise.
- `src/realtime/heartbeat.ts` — ping/pong scheduler and dead-peer reaper.
- `src/realtime/router.ts` — envelope validation, per-connection rate limit, dispatch.

| M5 | Multi-instance with Redis pub/sub, two-instance integration test | 7h |
| M6 | Reconnect and catch-up: jittered backoff, gap replay, client dedupe | 6h |
| M7 | Backpressure and rate limits: high-water policy, slow-consumer close | 4h |
| M8 | Client UI: conversation list, virtualised messages, optimistic send, status | 10h |

`429` error frames; a schema version handshake; autoscaling on connection count; a load balancer with

asserts recovery via catch-up; structured logs with `connectionId` and `conversationId`; and an ADR on

instance dies with messages in flight. It proves you understand the handshake, auth, heartbeat,
close codes, and reconnect with backoff; that you understand horizontal scale, since one node is not a
system; that you can reason about delivery guarantees and per-conversation ordering; and that you can

**Requirements**

*Must-have*

  for durable messages, Redis 7 for presence, fan-out, and rate limiting.
- 🟢 Authenticate during the handshake — verify a short-lived JWT before `upgrade`, and reject with
  the correct HTTP status. Never authenticate after accepting.
- 🟢 Conversations: 1:1 and group; a user joins only conversations they belong to; authorization
  checked on `join` and on every `send`.
- 🟢 Client-generated `clientMessageId` (UUID) with a unique constraint on
  `(conversationId, clientMessageId)`, so a retry never duplicates; the server assigns the
  authoritative id, `seq`, and `createdAt` and broadcasts the server record.
- 🟢 Ordering: a per-conversation gap-free sequence allocated under a row lock, with client-side gap
  detection and repair on reconnect.
- 🟢 Presence: online/offline/away with `presence:{userId}` and a ~45s TTL refreshed by the heartbeat,

- 🟢 Tests: unit for the message service and ordering; a two-instance integration test against one
