- *Evening + weekend (12–14h)*: Mon–Thu 90 minutes each, 45 of new concept and 45 of DSA or
  review. Fri off. Sat 4h project. Sun 2.5h project plus 1h review and planning.
- *Micro-sessions (6–8h)*: six 45-minute sessions — Mon, Tue, Thu DSA or recall; Wed reading; Sat
  2h; Sun 2h project. Never asks for a 3-hour evening, so it wins on consistency and loses on depth.
- *Two protected weekend blocks (10–12h)*: Sat and Sun 09:00–13:00 with zero weekday study. Two
  high-quality four-hour beats beat fourteen mediocre evenings.

**Rules that make 13 hours a week work for 24 weeks**

- **Never skip twice.** One missed week is an accident; two is a habit ending.
- **Fixed anchors** — the same four evenings and two weekend mornings every week. Decision fatigue
  kills plans, not time.
- **A 20-minute minimum viable session**: one DSA problem, 20 flashcards, or one chapter. A bad day
  still gets the floor, so the streak survives.
- **Two-week sprints, not monthly** — a named deliverable per two weeks.
- **Never mix DSA and project work in one session.** The switching cost is larger than most people
  estimate.
- **Sunday: review, then plan.** Thirty minutes of closed-book recall and thirty of planning, in
  writing. This is what makes the plan adapt rather than drift.
- **Track hours, review monthly.** The useful question is which slot produced the most retained
  material.
- **Sleep over study, always.** Fatigue destroys retrieval more than knowledge, and retrieval is
  what interviews test.
- **Tell one person.** Social accountability is the strongest predictor of a 24-week streak.
- **Take one real week off every eight.** Burnout at week 14 is why 6-month plans end at week 11.

**What to cut when behind, in order**: new concepts you have not applied (cut breadth, keep depth);
never mock interviews; weekend project time before evening sessions; drop DSA difficulty to
easy/medium but never drop DSA; cut reading entirely.

**The job-search overlay**

| Phase | Change |
| --- | --- |
| 8 weeks before applying | no change; the portfolio is the deliverable |
| Active search | −30% study, +30% applications and mocks; keep one evening of DSA and the weekend block; never both gone |
| After a rejection | +2h targeted repair; write down exactly which questions you missed — the repair is usually 3–5 hours |
| Between interviews | −20%; recovery is part of the plan, not a failure of it |
| Offer stage | −60%; negotiate from a rested position |

**The honest arithmetic**: at 13 hours a week, 13 × 52 = 676 hours a year — about what a
full-time employed person spends at their job. Your side project is a part-time job and should be
scoped like one: one project, one deliverable per week, no heroics. Anyone promising six portfolio
projects on 10 hours a week while working full time plans to fail in month three. One project done
properly beats four half-finished, and it is the one that gets interviews.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**What the role is**: you own the interface layer — rendering, state, accessibility, performance,
and the boundary to the API. Usually the last person to touch a pixel and the first to feel a
regression.

**What is weighted**

| Area | Weight | Depth needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JavaScript and TypeScript | Very high | Language semantics, event loop, types, module system |
| Browser platform | Very high | Rendering pipeline, events, storage, workers, caching |
| CSS and layout | High | Box model, flexbox, grid, custom properties, containment |
| Accessibility | High | Semantics, keyboard, focus, ARIA used sparingly, testing method |
| State management | High | Local versus server state, optimistic UI, form state, normalisation |
| Testing | High | Component tests, e2e, what not to test, mocking discipline |
| Framework depth | High | One framework's rendering model, not five APIs |
| Performance | Medium-high | Profiling, bundle size, code splitting, hydration cost, Core Web Vitals |
| System design | Medium | Client-heavy concerns: caching, CDN, auth, BFF, API aggregation |
| Server | Low-medium | Enough to talk to the API designer; not enough to own the schema |

**Projects that matter**: X.1.1 (non-negotiable; it is your first screen), X.1.3 (state beyond a
prototype), X.1.4 (a real product surface). X.1.8 differentiates on frontend-heavy AI teams.

**Questions you will be asked**

- "Why did this component re-render?" Expect state identity, referential equality, context value
  identity, and how you narrowed the update.
- "How do you decide what is server state and what is client state?" Expect a source of truth per
  datum, cache invalidation, and why duplicating server state into a store causes bugs.
- "How do you make this accessible without adding ARIA everywhere?" Semantics first, ARIA only for
  what HTML cannot express, and how you test it.
- "Our LCP is 4.2s. Walk me through what you would do, in order." Measurement, then the waterfall,
  then the diagnosis, then the fix, then a regression guard.
- "How do you handle a form with 30 fields and three dependent dropdowns?" Schema-driven
  validation, server as authority, an error summary, field-level UX.
- "What is the hydration cost here, and what would you do for a mostly-static page?"
- "How do you test a component that talks to an API?" Mock at the boundary, assert user-visible
  behaviour, never implementation details.

**What gets you hired**: a portfolio that is fast, accessible, and looks designed, plus the ability
to explain *why* a rendering happened. Frontend is unusually kind to candidates with visible taste.
Be ready to defend a spacing scale, a type scale, and a motion decision.

**Common failure modes**: framework breadth with no depth (six APIs worth less than one rendering
model); accessibility claimed but not demonstrated; "I use Redux" as an answer to a state question;
performance as assertion — never "React is fast", say where you measured.

**Depth checklist**: you can explain the event loop and why an effect runs twice in development; you
can explain what `useMemo`/`useCallback` do and when they are a pessimisation; you have profiled a
real app and fixed something because of the profile; you have shipped an accessible feature with no
keyboard traps; you have a component test that fails for the right reason; you can explain
hydration, streaming SSR, and when you would choose each.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**What the role is**: you own the server, the data, and the system's behaviour under failure.
Usually the person who gets paged.

**What is weighted**

| Area | Weight | Depth needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Language runtime | Very high | Memory, concurrency, error handling, profiling |
| Data modelling and SQL | Very high | Constraints, indexes, isolation, query plans, migrations |
| API design | Very high | Resources, versioning, error contracts, pagination, idempotency |
| Reliability | Very high | Retries, timeouts, idempotency, failure modes, DLQs |
| Distributed systems | High | Consistency, replication, partitioning, queues, idempotent consumers |
| Data stores | High | Postgres internals, Redis semantics, what goes where and why |
| Observability | High | Logs versus metrics versus traces, RED, SLOs, debugging method |
| Security | High | Authn/authz, injection, SSRF, secrets, dependency risk |
| System design | Very high | The main event for backend loops |
| Frontend | Low | Enough to know where the API is wrong |

**Projects that matter**: X.1.3 (the backbone), X.1.6 (you can operate what you build), X.1.7 (the
strongest backend signal available). X.1.5 and X.1.4 work if you lean into concurrency and payments.

**Questions you will be asked**

- "Design a rate limiter." Token bucket with a diagram, where state lives, the failure mode when the
  state store is down, and the trade-off versus a sliding window log.
- "A user says their payment disappeared. Walk me through every state it could be in."
- "How do you migrate 200 million rows without downtime?"
- "What is your replication lag doing to your read-after-write guarantees?"
- "Explain isolation levels with a concrete anomaly for each."
- "How do you debug a production issue with only logs?" The method: structured logs, a request id,
  a hypothesis, a query, a narrowing, and when you reach for tracing.
- "What happens when a downstream service takes 30 seconds instead of 300ms?" Timeout, circuit
  breaker, bulkhead, backpressure, and what you return to the caller.

**What gets you hired**: a project where you can describe a real failure and what you changed. One
backend candidate with one well-told incident beats one with four tutorial projects.

**Common failure modes**: no SQL depth — if you cannot read a query plan, backend loops find out;
distributed systems as vocabulary rather than reasoning (say what breaks, not just which pattern);
treating the database as magic storage; no failure stories, so prepare at least three.

**Depth checklist**: you can read `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` and fix a query from it; you have written a
migration that would have broken a rolling deploy and fixed it; you can explain idempotency and
where it must hold; your project's observability stack can answer "who is affected"; you have a real
incident story with a timeline and a prevention; you can design in 45 minutes with a diagram and
defend each choice.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**What the role is**: you own a vertical slice — API, data, interface — end to end. The most common
title at small and mid companies, and the most underserved by candidates who over-specialise.

**What is weighted**

| Area | Weight | Depth needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feature delivery | Very high | Take a requirement and ship it without hand-holding |
| API and data design | High | As backend, minus internals |
| Frontend | High | As frontend, minus platform interners |
| Testing | High | End-to-end confidence across the stack |
| Debugging | Very high | The defining skill: something breaks somewhere and you find it |
| DevOps awareness | Medium-high | Deploy, read logs, write a migration |
| System design | Medium-high | Feature- and slice-level, not org-wide |
| Depth in one area | Medium | T-shape: one real depth, breadth elsewhere |

**Projects that matter**: X.1.3, X.1.6, X.1.7, and X.1.2 as the discipline baseline. The portfolio
story is a *product*: something a person can use, with the trade-offs documented.

**Questions you will be asked**

- "How do you decide whether a feature belongs on the server or the client?"
- "Walk me through a feature you shipped. What did you get wrong?"
- "How do you test across the boundary?" Contract tests, integration against a real DB, a small e2e
  suite for critical paths.
- "How do you debug when the bug is in three places?"
- "A PM wants a change tomorrow. What do you do?" Scoping, a spike, and what you would say no to.
- "What is the difference between your frontend's view of the truth and the database's?"

**What gets you hired**: shipped range plus honest trade-off reasoning. The interviewer's fear is a
candidate who needs both a frontend and a backend specialist; you remove it by naming the seam you
know least well and what you are doing about it.

**Common failure modes**: claiming full stack and demonstrating neither (two shallow halves are
worse than one deep half plus real breadth); no ownership narrative — "we built" is not an answer,
"I designed, I shipped, and here is what I would change" is; never deploying, when full stack means
owning the seams and seams break in production.

**Depth checklist**: you can add an API field and update every consumer without breaking anything;
you can write the migration, endpoint, component, and tests for one feature; you have debugged a real
cross-stack bug (a timezone mismatch, a cache inconsistency, a race); you have deployed and rolled
back something; you can name the three parts of your project you would redesign first.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**What the role is**: you solve whatever is in front of you this week. Scope is undefined, context
switching is constant, shipping speed beats elegance, and you are valued for judgment about what
*not* to build.

**What is weighted**

| Area | Weight | Depth needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Breadth across the stack | Very high | Self-sufficient across the whole surface |
| Speed and judgment | Very high | The core signal: can you tell what to skip? |
| Integrations | High | Third-party APIs, webhooks, OAuth, payments, imports/exports |
| Data modelling | High | The schema changes as the business learns, so migrations must be cheap |
| Operational independence | High | You deploy it, you page it, you fix it |
| Communication | Very high | Non-engineering stakeholders are your daily counterpart |
| System design | Medium | Right-sized: solve today's problem, name tomorrow's |
| Deep theory | Low | Theatrical complexity is actively negative here |

**Projects that matter**: X.1.4 (payments and admin — the classic startup build), X.1.6 (operating
your own thing), X.1.5 (real-time is common in product work), X.1.8 (AI features are a startup
default). Also anything integration-heavy with two third-party APIs.

**Questions you will be asked**

- "How do you decide what to build first?" Talk to users, find the constraint, pick the smallest
  thing that tests the assumption.
- "How do you integrate with a third-party API that will definitely fail?" Adapter pattern,
  idempotency, webhooks over polling, a manual override.
- "We need OAuth login by Friday. Go." Plan, libraries, failure modes (state, redirect, token
  storage, scope).
- "How do you handle a schema change with 10k rows on a hot table?"
- "Tell me about a time you shipped something wrong." Ownership, timeline, fix, prevention.
- "How do you keep yourself from over-engineering?" A heuristic, and a willingness to delete.

**What gets you hired**: velocity with judgment, and the words "I shipped it in three days and here
is the thing I know will bite us in six months". Startup interviews reward someone who can hold a
whole system in their head and still decide.

**Common failure modes**: over-engineering as a flex (show restraint instead); refusing ops work,
which at a startup *is* the job; ambiguity avoidance — the test is often deliberately vague and you
are expected to ask the clarifying questions yourself.

**Depth checklist**: you have integrated a third-party API with a webhook and handled replay; you
have shipped a schema change with zero downtime; you can scope a two-week feature into a two-day
version and say what you cut; you have been solely responsible for something running in production;
you have deleted your own feature and written down why.

- "How do you integrate with a third-party API that will definitely fail?" Adapter pattern,
  idempotency, webhooks over polling, a manual override.
- "We need OAuth login by Friday. Go." Plan, libraries, failure modes (state, redirect, token
  storage, scope).
- "How do you handle a schema change with 10k rows on a hot table?"
- "Tell me about a time you shipped something wrong." Ownership, timeline, fix, prevention.
- "How do you keep yourself from over-engineering?" A heuristic, and a willingness to delete.

**What gets you hired**: velocity with judgment, and the words "I shipped it in three days and here
is the thing I know will bite us in six months". Startup interviews reward someone who can hold a
whole system in their head and still decide.

**Common failure modes**: over-engineering as a flex (show restraint instead); refusing ops work,
which at a startup *is* the job; ambiguity avoidance — the test is often deliberately vague and you
are expected to ask the clarifying questions yourself.

**Depth checklist**: you have integrated a third-party API with a webhook and handled replay; you
have shipped a schema change with zero downtime; you can scope a two-week feature into a two-day

you have deleted your own feature and written down why.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
Most people have a current job and a mild preference, not a strong pull. Decide with evidence.

**Step 1 — the 60-question diagnostic by section.** Recompute per-section percentages from X.2.5
and look at the *shape*: JS/browser/CSS/React highest → frontend-leaning; SQL/data/API/reliability
highest → backend-leaning; all mid with one peak → T-shaped, peak as depth; all mid with no peak →
balanced full stack or startup generalist.

**Step 2 — the pleasure test, the most reliable signal.** Over two weeks, notice which you *want* to
do when nobody is grading you: making an interface feel instant and caring about 16ms; finding the
bug three layers down and caring about consistency; the moment a feature works end to end; or turning
a vague PM ask into a shipped thing. Take the signal — it is worth more than a salary spreadsheet.

**Step 3 — the constraint test.** 5 hours a week or 25? Frontend is learnable at 5; backend and
distributed systems usually are not. Is your current domain a strength? Five years in finance means
you are a credible backend candidate there and a mediocre frontend one. What help can you get?
Frontend colleagues review backend code and vice versa; feedback access beats theoretical fit.

**Step 4 — the 30-day trial.** Do not decide from a plan. Build 80% of X.1.1 in one weekend and 80%
of X.1.3 in another. Week 1: note which you *anticipated* and which you *finished*. Week 4: note
which problem you would rather have for a year. The gap between anticipation and completion,
repeated, is the answer.

**Step 5 — the market test, and its limits.** Read 30 postings per track in your city and band; count
required technologies, years, and how often the two actually differ. Frequently they do not —
"full stack" postings are 70% backend. Use the market as a tiebreaker between two things you
genuinely want, not as the primary signal, because markets move and tastes do not.

**Step 6 — when you genuinely cannot choose**, default to **balanced full stack**: the largest job
market, the fewest demands for prior depth, keeps both skills alive, and is easy to specialise from
later. The cost is being weaker than a specialist in one area for a year or two — usually fine and
usually forgotten by the time you are senior.

**Step 7 — how tracks change by level**

| Level | Frontend | Backend | Full stack | Generalist |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Junior | Framework fluency, CSS, a11y basics, one shipped project | SQL, REST, a deployed API | A full vertical slice | Shipping speed, small features end to end |
| Mid | Rendering, state, performance, testing, a11y depth | Data modelling, indexes, reliability, design | Slice-level design, testing, debugging | Integrations, judgment, ops independence |
| Senior | Large-frontend architecture, design systems, perf budgets | Data architecture, consistency, migrations at scale | Cross-service seams, technical leadership | Technical direction amid ambiguity |
| Staff | Org-wide frontend strategy, tooling, standards | Org-wide data and platform strategy | Org-wide architecture and trade-off frameworks | Company-level technical strategy |

**How to change tracks later, honestly**: tracks are not identities. Backend→frontend is three to
six months of deliberate work; frontend→backend is six to twelve because SQL and data modelling
compound more slowly. Frontend→full stack is easiest; backend→frontend at senior level is hardest
because you are assessed against a rendering-model depth bar. Plan the transition as a project —
one substantial build in the new track plus a targeted gap plan from the diagnostic.

groups.title: Level Tracks
groups.description:
Level Tracks within Cross-cutting Tracks and the Final Interview Kit.

---

What changes as you go up is not the size of your answers; it is **the axis of judgement**. Junior:
do the thing correctly. Mid: do it well under constraints. Senior: choose between good options and
live with the consequences. Staff: decide whether the team should be doing this at all.

| Level | Judged on | Can articulate | Typical failure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Junior | Correctness, learning velocity, fundamentals | "It works; here is how I tested it" | Cannot explain why, only that |
| Mid | Scope, trade-offs, quality, debugging | "Three options; here is why this one; here is what it costs" | Executes the task as specified and misses the real problem |
| Senior | Design, judgement, risk, influence | "Here is the system we should build, and what happens when it is wrong" | Excellent work that solves the wrong problem |
| Staff | Cross-team, org-level, strategy, leverage | "Here is the org-wide constraint, and why the local optimum is a trap" | A ticket router, or a hero who blocks on themselves |

The practical test at each level: **at what scope can you decide without asking permission?**
Junior: within the task. Mid: within the feature. Senior: within the system. Staff: within the
portfolio of systems and the goals they serve.

Explain how junior interviews run and when you would use it.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**The bar**: you can be trusted with a well-specified task inside a codebase someone else designed,
and you find out you were wrong early and say so. Everything below is calibration for that.

**Fundamentals you must have**: your language (types, scope, closures, modules, async, error
handling, immutability, reading unfamiliar code); the platform (browser rendering or your runtime's
concurrency and I/O); HTTP verbs, headers, status codes, and a request's whole lifecycle; data
(`SELECT` with joins, DML, indexes and why they help, transactions, reading a schema); Git (branch,
commit, rebase, resolve a conflict, read a diff); testing (write a unit test, run a suite, read a
failure); one framework used properly; and enough accessibility or operability not to ship broken
keyboard navigation.

**DSA**: easy and early-medium from a defined set — arrays, strings, hash maps, stacks, linked
lists, simple trees, plus the patterns two pointers, sliding window, and basic BFS/DFS. 60–80
problems total, comfortable rather than fast. You must narrate.

**Project**: one, done properly — X.1.2 for a TypeScript target, X.1.1 for pure frontend. Done
means deployed, tested, and a README saying what it is and what you would improve.

**How junior interviews run**: recruiter screen (30 min — motivation, salary, notice; prepare three
sentences on why this company and role); technical screen (45–60 min, often one small problem, the
bar being "working solution plus thinking out loud"); onsite (two coding rounds, one fundamentals
round over language/HTTP/databases, one behavioural); and a project walkthrough where they will ask
"why did you do it this way" about three decisions — prepare three.

**The four questions every junior candidate fails**

1. "Tell me about a project." They ramble for four minutes. Prepare 90 seconds: problem, what you
   built, one hard decision, one thing you would change.
2. "Why this technology?" They say "it was in the tutorial". Prepare one real answer per technology,
   including the alternative you rejected.
3. "What happens when you type a URL and press enter?" They stop at "it goes to the server".
4. "Where do you want to grow?" They say "senior in five years". Say what you want to be *good at*.

**What gets a junior hired**: visible learning velocity, fundamentals that survive questioning, a
project you can discuss with self-awareness, and the ability to say "I don't know; here's how I'd
find out" without panicking.

**Anti-patterns**: frameworks before the language; a portfolio of half-finished clones; certificates
without artifacts; not reading your own code (the highest-return junior habit); claiming a tool you
have never run.

**A 12-month junior checklist**: 80 narrated DSA problems, 40 without hints; one project shipped,
tested, documented, improved after feedback; three books end to end (language, platform, DSA);
ten technical blog posts read and three written; one hour a week reading your own old code; two
recorded mock interviews a month with written debriefs.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain what must have and when you would use it.
Explain how mid interviews run and when you would use it.
Explain how to answer a system design round, precisely and when you would use it.
Explain what gets a mid hired and when you would use it.
Explain anti-patterns and when you would use it.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**The bar**: trusted with a whole feature — design included — across the stack, and you raise the
right problems before they become someone else's. Communication is now a technical skill you are
assessed on.

**What must have**

- **Frameworks**: two used in anger. You can explain each rendering model and where each is a poor
  fit. You have debugged a framework-level problem (a stale closure, a hydration mismatch, a
  connection leak).
- **Databases**: schema design with real constraints, indexing from first principles, transactions
  and isolation, migrations as a discipline, query-plan reading.
- **Testing**: unit, integration, contract, e2e; what to test and what to mock; a test that caught a
  real bug; a suite fast enough that people run it.
- **System design basics**: statelessness, load balancing, caching layers, database scale-up versus
  scale-out, queues, consistency models — enough for one 45-minute round.
- **Reliability**: retries with backoff, idempotency, timeouts, health checks, structured logging,
  reading a dashboard during an incident.
- **Security**: authn/authz, injection, XSS, CSRF, secret handling, dependency risk.
- **Code quality**: reviewable diffs, small commits, tests that matter, refactoring with the change.

**DSA**: easy/medium confidently, medium/hard with structure — arrays, strings, hash maps, heaps,
linked lists, trees, graphs, basic DP, and monotonic-stack patterns. 120–150 problems total.
Speed matters: 25–30 minutes for a medium.

**Project**: two, or one substantial one. X.1.3 plus X.1.6 (containerising it) is a coherent mid
story: a real app, properly operated. Add X.1.2 if your discipline is weak.

**How mid interviews run**: recruiter plus a 45-minute technical screen with real depth; onsite with
one medium coding round, one system design round (45 min), one project deep-dive with hostile
follow-ups, one behavioural round. The design round separates mids — it is not about knowing the
answer but about clarifying, drawing, and changing your mind out loud. The deep-dive is the second
filter: they pick one thing and press for twenty minutes, and if you did not do it you run out of
things to say.

**How to answer a system design round, precisely**

1. **Clarify (5 min)**: functional requirements, users, scale in numbers, consistency needs. Write
   the numbers down; they anchor everything.
2. **Requirements (3 min)**: what must be true versus optional.
3. **Estimate (3 min)**: DAU, requests/second, storage, bandwidth. Rounded is fine — they want
   orders of magnitude.
4. **Draw the high level (10 min)**: clients, edge, services, stores, arrows with protocols. Say the
   data model out loud.
5. **Deepen (15 min)**: the write path, the consistency boundary, the hot spot. If asked to "design
   X", ask which part matters.
6. **Failure and scale (9 min)**: what happens when a component dies, a dependency slows, traffic is
   100×. This is where mids lose points.
7. **Trade-offs (5 min)**: name what you gave up.

Mid-plus signals: you start from the read path because 95% of traffic is reads; keyset pagination for
a deep list; a cache with named invalidation; you ask about consistency before choosing a database;
you notice that a queue means retries, so idempotency is now mandatory. Junior signals: designing
before clarifying; one big database box; "we can add caching later" with no invalidation story; no
numbers anywhere.

**What gets a mid hired**: depth in one area plus honest breadth, a project with a defensible
trade-off, and the ability to think out loud without needing to be right. Mids are hired for
*velocity and judgment*, and judgment shows as proportionality — solving the asked problem well.

**Anti-patterns**: system design as vocabulary; optimising what nobody asked about; a project you
cannot demo in five minutes; ignoring the human side (no estimate, no plan, no narration).

**A 12-month mid checklist**: 150 narrated DSA problems with a documented pattern log; two shipped
projects with CI, monitoring, and a decision log; 30 design problems with written scaling sections;
ten behavioural STAR stories covering conflict, failure, ambiguity, feedback, impact; leading one
technical end to end (design, rollout, monitoring); weekly code review that teaches someone.

---

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**The bar**: trusted with outcomes rather than tasks. You choose the approach, you carry the risk,
and you make other people more effective. You are evaluated on whether the work you owned still
works six months later, and on whether two engineers are better because you were there.

**What must have**

- **Design depth at two zooms**: the macro design (services, stores, consistency boundaries,
  deployment topology) and the micro design (the algorithm, the query, the lock, the buffer). You
  name failure modes before they are named for you.
- **Architecture judgment**: you know when a monolith is right and can give the three signals that
  it has stopped working, so you are not a microservices evangelist.
- **Trade-off fluency**: you can defend either side of any architectural question because you
  understand the axes — consistency versus availability, latency versus throughput, build versus buy,
  cost versus latency, simplicity versus flexibility.
- **Data architecture**: modelling a domain deeply, evolving schemas without downtime, and
  understanding replication, partitioning, and retention.
- **Reliability and operations**: SLOs, error budgets, incident command, blameless postmortems,
  capacity planning, a rollback you have performed.
- **Security as a designer**: threat modelling, least privilege, defaults that are safe.
- **Technical communication**: design docs people read, RFCs that get decisions made, the same
  thing explained at three levels to three audiences.
- **Leverage**: code review that teaches, runbooks others can use, onboarding that shortens a ramp.

**The twelve senior design topics you must reason about**

1. Scaling a read-heavy system: caches at every layer, CDN, cache keys, invalidation, stampede
   protection, staleness budgets.
2. Scaling a write-heavy system: partitioning keys, hot partitions, write amplification, queueing to
   smooth, batching.
3. Consistency and replication: primary/replica, read-after-write, quorum reads, eventual
   consistency as a user perceives it.
4. Sharding and rebalancing: choosing a key, rebalancing, behaviour during a move, why the shard key
   cannot change.
5. Queues and asynchronous work: delivery guarantees, ordering, duplicate handling, backpressure,
   DLQs, idempotent consumers.
6. Failure and resilience: timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, retries with jitter, graceful
   degradation, behaviour when a dependency dies.
7. Storage selection: relational versus document versus key-value versus wide-column versus search,
   and the access patterns forcing each.
8. Multi-tenancy and isolation: the three models, their costs, and noisy neighbours.
9. Auth, authorisation, and multi-region identity: sessions, tokens, SSO, federation, revocation.
10. Observability and operations: what to measure, RED versus USE, SLOs, alerts that do not cry wolf,
   debugging under uncertainty.
11. Security architecture: threat modelling, secrets, encryption at rest and in transit, supply chain,
   incident response.
12. Cost and capacity: modelling, unit economics, performance versus spend.

For each: a diagram, three options with named trade-offs, a failure-mode list, and "what changes at
100×".

**How senior interviews run**: recruiter, then a 60-minute system design or architecture round; then
an onsite with one design round (45–60 min), one deep code review or debugging round, one
project/architecture deep-dive, and one cross-team influence round. The differentiator is the
influence-and-ambiguity round: "a technical decision others disagreed with", or "here is a mess you
inherited — what do you do first?" Code is less central than at mid; reading and reviewing code, and
talking about a system you did not build, matter more.

**What a senior deep-dive looks like**: you are handed your own project from two years ago,
described only by a diagram, and asked to walk it. What they are testing: can you explain past
decisions without defensiveness, including the ones you would change; do you know your system's
failure modes and have you seen any occur; do you know the operational story (how do you know it is
healthy, how do you ship a change, what happens at 3am); and do you know what you would redesign, and
can you justify it by what changed in the business rather than by taste. The strongest answer includes
something you would *remove*. Senior engineers talk about subtraction.

**How to answer "tell me about a trade-off you made"**: context in one sentence (scale, constraints,
what was at stake); the options you genuinely considered, including the rejected one and why; the
decision with the specific reason, usually a constraint rather than a preference; what it cost you,
concretely; and what would make you revisit it. That last part is what seniors add and mids miss.

**What gets a senior hired**: demonstrable judgment, systems that survived real traffic and real
incidents, and the ability to raise the quality bar for people around you. Also: being the person
who is not the loudest in the room and still lands the right call.

**Anti-patterns**: architecture as a solution to a problem nobody has — over-design is the
senior-level failure mode where mids under-design; rewriting instead of evolving (a rewrite is almost
always a status move); "I would have done X differently" with no constraint; heroics at 2am, which
hides the design problem that will recur; mentoring as a status label rather than measured by the
other person's growth.

**A 12-month senior checklist**: 40 design problems written up with a scaling section and failure
modes; two production incidents handled with written blameless postmortems and a preventive change
you shipped; one design doc that changed a team's direction, including the political work to adopt
it; two engineers visibly levelled up; an SLO for a service you own with an error budget gating
deploys; and a written retrospective on your last two quarters including what you stopped doing.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain what must have and when you would use it.
Explain what the interviews actually test and when you would use it.
Explain concrete differences from senior and when you would use it.
Explain anti-patterns and when you would use it.
Explain evidence to build in year one and when you would use it.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**The bar**: you affect systems you do not own, teams you do not manage, and a horizon measured in
years. You are evaluated on leverage — how much other people's throughput and quality improve
because you exist — and on whether the organisation is pointed at the right problem.

**What must have**

- **Org-wide architecture**: multi-region, multi-team data and service boundaries, and the
  organisational constraints (team ownership, on-call, compliance) that determine which technical
  options are even available.
- **Strategy as a written artefact**: a multi-year technical bet tied to revenue, cost, or risk, with
  milestones and *kill criteria*.
- **Decision frameworks**: reusable ways of thinking that others apply to new problems — not one-off
  opinions. The test is whether a team uses your doc as a template without you.
- **Influence without authority**: aligning teams that do not report to you, resolving genuine
  conflicts of interest, and being able to say "no" upward with evidence.
- **Compounding leverage**: you have grown seniors who are now growing others. Your success is their
  promotion.
- **Risk literacy**: knowing which org-wide risks deserve retirement now (compliance, the migration,
  the incident class, the vendor lock-in) and which can wait.
- **Organisational design**: team boundaries, role design, hiring calibration, the level bar.

**What the interviews actually test**

- **Scope decomposition**: given a slow org, produce a portfolio of bets with sequencing and a
  narrative about why the order matters.
- **Disagreement resolution**: two teams' proposals conflict; you must find a decision both can live
  with, and articulate the principle behind it.
- **Long-horizon judgement**: a technology migration three years out — what do you commit to now, and
  what do you deliberately defer?
- **Self-awareness about failure**: what org-wide bet did you get wrong, and what did it cost, and
  what did you change about how you bet?

**Concrete differences from senior**

| Dimension | Senior | Staff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Optimisation horizon | one to two quarters | one to three years |
| Change mechanism | you design it well and people follow the design | you build the decision framework and the coalition |
| Blast radius of a bad call | a system | several teams and possibly a migration |
| Primary output | designs and reviews | strategies, RFCs, decision records, and grown people |
| Success measure | the system works | other teams are faster and better, and the bet paid off |

**Anti-patterns**: architecture for its own sake; meetings as the deliverable; becoming the approval
bottleneck everyone routes through; depth without breadth, becoming the person who knows one system
perfectly; strategy that is really a technology preference in a longer document.

**Evidence to build in year one**: one cross-team architectural change (something three teams had to
coordinate — it will take longer, and that is the job); a decision framework others reuse; technical
strategy tied to a business metric; leaders grown into seniors whom you actively work on and take
credit for; an org-level risk retired; and hiring and team design where you set the level bar.

---

interviewQuestions.text: Explain a concrete rubric, so you can self-assess and when you would use it.
Explain the same three questions, asked differently and when you would use it.
Explain common to every level and when you would use it.
Explain signals you are being considered for the next level and when you would use it.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**A concrete rubric, so you can self-assess**

| Dimension | Junior | Mid | Senior | Staff |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scope of decisions | Within the task | Within the feature | Within the system | Across systems and goals |
| Problem framing | Accepts the problem as stated | Asks a clarifying question | Reframes the problem and says why | Reframes the portfolio and the goal |
| Design | Follows an existing pattern | Chooses a pattern | Argues for a pattern and a cost | Sets a standard others follow |
| Implementation | Correct, readable | Correct, tested, reviewable | Tested, instrumented, rollback-safe | Leaves the codebase better than found |
| Failure | Fixes the bug | Prevents the class | Designs so the class cannot recur | Designs the org to see it sooner |
| Communication | Answers in the thread | Writes the plan | Writes the doc that unblocks a team | Aligns organisations around a direction |
| Influence | Answers questions | Reviews a PR well | Raises the level of a team | Raises the level of several teams |
| Judgement under ambiguity | Asks for a spec | Writes a small spec | Makes the call and documents it | Makes the call that changes the game |
| Operational ownership | Runs it locally | Deploys it | Owns it in production, page and all | Owns the platform others own things on |
| Hiring | Passes their bar | Raises the bar | Gets others hired well | Builds the hiring system |
| Self-improvement | Learns quickly | Deliberately practises | Teaches deliberately | Raises the team's capability system |

**The same three questions, asked differently**

- *"Why did you do it that way?"* — Junior: "that is the tutorial pattern." Mid: "X is constrained
  by Y." Senior: "Z cost more than we could justify, and here is the condition under which I would
  switch." Staff: "We chose a portfolio posture of optimising for reversibility, and here is how I
  know it worked."
- *"What happens if this breaks?"* — Junior: "we fix it." Mid: "tests and monitoring." Senior:
  "fails closed, pages the on-call, runbook at this link, rollback takes four minutes, and I have
  run it." Staff: "blast radius bounded by tenant, we degrade to the last-known-good path, and the
  error budget tells us whether we ship the next thing."
- *"How do you know it worked?"* — Junior: "the tests pass." Mid: "metrics moved." Senior: "the
  SLO held and the error budget did not spend." Staff: "the predicted outcome is the measured
  outcome, and the ones we got wrong are written down."

**Common to every level**: communication, ownership, and judgement. The level changes how much
ambiguity each absorbs. A junior who communicates clearly and asks good questions is hired faster
than a mid who is silent and correct.

**Signals you are being considered for the next level**: you are invited to *design* reviews rather
than attend; you are asked "how would you do this" rather than "can you do this"; people outside your
team ask you questions; you are asked to review a design document; you are asked to represent the
team externally. If you want the next level, the fastest route is usually not more individual
output — it is taking ownership of something whose outcome you could not previously influence, and
carrying it visibly.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
Promotion is not a conversation you have; it is a body of evidence you accumulate and can point at.
Assume you were hired at the level named.

**Junior — year one evidence**

| Evidence | Why it counts | How to build it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5–8 shipped features, small to medium | Delivery reliability | Volunteer for the ticket nobody wants; ship it fully including tests and docs |
| One feature improved after feedback | Coachability | Ask for the review, take one piece seriously, show the diff |
| A bug found before it shipped | Quality instinct | Read other people's PRs; say "this breaks if" once you are sure |
| A growth narrative with specifics | Velocity | Keep a private log: what you did not know in month 1 versus month 12, with evidence |
| Questions that improve the team | Contribution | A one-page note on a repeated mistake, shared without ego |
| A side project | Sustained effort | One thing, finished, with a README |
| Asking for help early and well | Communication | "I'm stuck on X; here is what I tried; here is my hypothesis" — practise it |

Anti-evidence: shipping volume without quality; visibility instead of usefulness; avoiding ambiguity;
learning alone because asking felt slow.

**Mid — year one evidence**

| Evidence | Why it counts | How to build it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2–3 features owned end to end | Ownership | Volunteer for the feature with messy requirements and cross-team dependencies |
| A design doc that changed a plan | Technical judgement | Write it before you start; circulate, take the disagreement, revise, cite the decision |
| A production incident you handled | Operational judgement | Volunteer to be first responder once; write the timeline afterwards |
| Test coverage that catches real bugs | Quality | A regression test for every bug you fix; count them |
| Two code reviews that taught something | Leverage | Comments that explain why, not what; track who thanked you |
| A performance or cost improvement with a number | Measurement | Profile something, fix it, report before and after |
| A decision others disagreed with | Ability to act | Take a stance with reasons, write the risk down, check the outcome |
| Mentored someone through something hard | Multiplier | Pair on their worst task; do not take over |

Anti-evidence: the person who always says yes; avoiding design discussions; hoarding context;
technical excellence in a project nobody uses.

**Senior — year one evidence**

| Evidence | Why it counts | How to build it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A system you redesigned with a measured outcome | Architectural impact | Propose it, quantify the baseline, ship incrementally, publish the numbers |
| SLOs and an error budget you own | Operational maturity | Add them to a service nobody was measuring; tie release policy to the budget |
| A blameless postmortem that changed practice | Learning culture | Write it, run the review, ship the preventive change, then say so |
| Cross-team technical alignment | Influence | Get two teams to agree a contract or standard; write down why |
| 2–3 engineers visibly levelled up | Multiplication | Take someone through a design decision, a presentation, a review, a failure |
| Removed something | Judgement | Kill a service, a flag, a dependency, a process; write the postmortem on the deletion |
| A recurring incident class eliminated | Systemic thinking | Find the pattern across three incidents and fix the class |
| Standards followed without enforcement | Leverage | A template, a checklist, a lint rule, a paved road people choose |
| A written retrospective you acted on | Self-awareness | Quarterly, with specifics, including what you stopped doing |

Anti-evidence: heroics; being the single point of failure; redesigns as identity; influence that is

## Part 4 — Interpretation and traps

- **High score, low confidence is a warning, not a strength** — you are pattern-matching. Fix with
  closed-book re-tests a week apart.
- **A low DSA score does not mean junior.** Some strong seniors are slow at DSA. Check what the
  target loop actually weighs.
- **High G score with slow time is fragile.** Two minutes per problem means recalling a template;
  interrogate yourself with "what would change if this constraint changed?".
- **Section I below 40% is a blocker.** Re-do it before any other study, at any level.
- **Re-test in four weeks.** The trend is the measurement; keep the first one and compare honestly.
- **Never take this with notes open.** It measures recognition, not what you need.

| --- | --- | --- |
| A and B high, D and E low | 🟢 Frontend-leaning (X.3.1) | D, E to working knowledge; keep A and B sharp |
| D and E high, F low | 🔴 Backend-leaning (X.3.2) | F to working knowledge; A stays critical |
| A, C, D, F all mid-high, none above 85% | Balanced full stack (X.3.3) | Highest section becomes your T-depth |
| F, C, I, H high, G mid, high shipping velocity | Startup generalist (X.3.4) | G is the growth edge; I is the differentiator |
| Everything mid, nothing below 60% | Choose by the pleasure test (X.3.5 Step 2) | Breadth now, depth later |
| I or H below 40% | Any track, but fix this first | A security or operability gap is a hard blocker |

**Step 3**: pick a target *level*, not just a track, using J, G, and E as the signal.

| Signal | Level |
| --- | --- |
| J under 40%, G under 40%, I or H under 40% | Junior. Do not interview for mid yet |
| J 40–70%, G 50–75%, D 60%+ with reasoning | Mid |
| J 70%+, G 70%+, E 75%+, you can talk about failures and trade-offs | Senior |
| J and G both 85%+, plus cross-team technical leadership in the last year | Staff |

**Step 4**: write the plan. For each of your bottom two sections write the exact thing you cannot
do, the artifact that proves it closed, and the week it happens. Then take the relevant path from
X.2: 2-week, 8-week, 6-month, or 12-month.

---

## Part 4 — Interpretation and traps

- **High score, low confidence is a warning, not a strength** — you are pattern-matching. Fix with
  closed-book re-tests a week apart.
- **A low DSA score does not mean junior.** Some strong seniors are slow at DSA. Check what the
  target loop actually weighs.
- **High G score with slow time is fragile.** Two minutes per problem means recalling a template;
  interrogate yourself with "what would change if this constraint changed?".
- **Section I below 40% is a blocker.** Re-do it before any other study, at any level.
- **Re-test in four weeks.** The trend is the measurement; keep the first one and compare honestly.
- **Never take this with notes open.** It measures recognition, not what you need.

---

## Part 5 — The one-page summary, rewritten monthly

```
Date: ____________
Target role: ____________________  Target level: ________  Target company set: __________

Top two strengths (with evidence):
  1. _____________________________________________  evidence: ______________
  2. _____________________________________________  evidence: ______________

Bottom two gaps (with the artifact that closes each):
  1. _____________________________________________  closes when: __________
  2. _____________________________________________  closes when: __________

Project story in 90 seconds (problem / what I built / one hard decision / one thing I would change):
  ______________________________________________________________________________

Three questions I will be asked that I cannot yet answer:
  1. ___________________________________________________________________________
  2. ___________________________________________________________________________
  3. ___________________________________________________________________________

Weekly hours I can genuinely sustain: ______  Fixed anchors: _______________________

Next 90-day deliverable: ________________________________________________________________
```

---

A reusable rubric per stage so you grade a build before an interviewer does. Use it strictly, and
twice — once mid-build, once after you think you are done.

**How to use**: 0–4 per dimension, no halves (they invite negotiation with yourself). Score each
dimension before looking at any example answer. A 0 or 1 is a rewrite, not a fix; two 1s means stop
and rebuild. Re-score after 48 hours away — fatigue hides gaps.

| Score | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Absent or wrong |
| 1 | Present, but only at the tutorial level |
| 2 | Correct and conventional; a reviewer would approve |
| 3 | Correct, non-obvious choices, each justifiable |
| 4 | Production-shaped, measured, with limits and a next evolution named |

---

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**The three-mock rotation.** Do not do the same mock format three times. Rotate the *interviewer persona*, the *problem source*, and the *feedback latency* so you train three different failure modes.

| Mock type | Who plays interviewer | Time | What it trains |
|---|---|---|---|
| Peer mock (live call) | A friend, using the scorecard verbatim | 60 min | Speaking under mild social pressure |
| Recorded self mock | Yourself, webcam on, timer on | 45–60 min | Content quality without social pressure |
| AI mock (transcript reviewed) | Any tool, transcript after | 30 min | Volume and no-feedback tolerance |
| Strict interviewer | Senior dev who gives almost no feedback until the end | 60 min | Resilience to non-rewarding environments |

**Pre-flight checklist (5 minutes before you start).**

1. Close Slack, email, IDE notifications, and every other tab. Physically unplug if you can.
2. Water within arm's reach. Two minutes of throat-clearing cough costs more than you think.
3. Screen share the correct window. Nobody wants to watch you hunt for the repo.
4. Share your scratchpad application and make sure it renders for the other person (contrast, font size).
5. Write down the three numbers you must hit before you start: minutes per phase, your target score, and the one skill you are deliberately drilling.
6. If recorded: confirm audio, confirm the recording started, note the timestamp of the start in a text file.

**Timing template for a 60-minute full loop.**

| Window | Phase | Your job |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00–0:04 | Introductions + resume framing | Name your two strongest projects in one sentence each. Set the agenda. |
| 0:04–0:19 | Coding | Clarify, then code, then test. Narrate the whole time. |
| 0:19–0:34 | System design | Drive. Ask questions. Whiteboard the data path. |
| 0:34–0:46 | Behavioral | Two STAR stories minimum. One failure story is mandatory. |
| 0:46–0:58 | Deep dive / your questions | Your questions should reveal depth, not ask about benefits. |
| 0:58–1:00 | Close | Thank them, ask about next steps, write down every observation. |

For a 45-minute loop: coding 15, design 12, behavioral 8, questions 8. For a 90-minute loop: coding 30, design 25, behavioral 20, deep dive 12.

**The recording protocol.** Record audio only for the first three mocks — video feels like a punishment and suppresses your output. Transcribe or skim within 2 hours, while the pain is fresh. Mark every sentence where you said filler openers ("so", "basically", "you know", "like") and every place you went silent for more than five seconds. Those two counts are your real metrics.

**Feedback protocol.** Whoever interviews you must fill the scorecard *while* interviewing, not from memory afterwards. Memory rewrites harsh feedback into encouragement and you lose the signal. Ask for exactly three things: your score per rubric dimension, the one thing to fix, and one thing that was already fine (so you do not over-correct).

**Environment variable to fix if it is wrong.** If your mocks are easier than the real thing, you are not ready for the real thing. Add latency: use a shared doc with 200 ms of lag, or have the interviewer interrupt with follow-ups at unpredictable times.

keyConcepts: Automatic fail flags
Common score patterns and what they mean

interviewQuestions.text: Explain automatic fail flags and when you would use it.
Explain common score patterns and what they mean and when you would use it.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
Score each dimension 1–5. A hire signal is typically 3+ on coding with no 1s and no 2s on communication.

| # | Dimension | 1 (bad) | 3 (solid) | 5 (excellent) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | Requirements clarification | Starts coding immediately, misses a hard constraint | Asks 3–4 questions, catches scope and data-shape issues | Drives clarification: probes edge cases, non-functional requirements, and the intended user, then restates the spec |
| C2 | Data structure choice | Picks the obvious one and hopes | Picks a reasonable structure and can justify it | Derives the structure from the access pattern and names the complexity of each operation |
| C3 | Algorithm correctness | Wrong on the main case | Correct on main case, misses one edge case | Correct on all cases, including empties, duplicates, negatives, and overflow-scale inputs |
| C4 | Implementation fluency | Cannot write a loop without heavy fumbling | Writes working code, moderate lookup pauses | Fluent, clean, idiomatic, uses standard library helpers appropriately |
| C5 | Complexity analysis | Silent, or claims the wrong complexity | States time and space complexity correctly for the final solution | States complexity per operation, explains the trade-off that led to the choice, and notes what breaks it |
| C6 | Testing discipline | Never runs code | Runs the happy path and one edge case | Writes explicit test cases first or alongside, covers edge and boundary cases, verifies failures are handled |
| C7 | Iterability | Defends the first solution | Accepts a hint, adapts | Reaches a correct solution, then improves it unprompted |
| C8 | Communication under pressure | Silent for minutes, defensive | Mostly narrated, occasional long pauses | Continuous narration of intent: "now I need to find the window, so I'll do a two-pointer" |
| C9 | Readability | Variable names like `x1`, `tmp2` | Readable names, some nesting | Clear names, small functions, early returns, no dead code |
| C10 | Time management | Runs out of time mid-solution | Finishes with a rushed edge case | Ships a correct simpler solution early, then hardens and optimizes |

**Automatic fail flags.** Wrong answer with no self-caught bug after 15 minutes of your own testing. Blaming the interviewer. Silent for more than 10 minutes. Coding in a file you cannot explain afterwards.

**Common score patterns and what they mean.**

| Pattern | Diagnosis | Next 7 days |
|---|---|---|
| C6 high, C1 low | You can code, you cannot listen. Most common mid-level failure. | Do 15 "spec-first" drills: given a LeetCode-style prompt, write only questions for 5 minutes |
| C2 low, C3 high | Lucky guesses with weak fundamentals. | Re-derive the canonical solutions for your top 20 patterns from scratch |
| C5 high, C2 low | You analyze complexity but choose badly. | For each of 25 problems, write the access-pattern table before solving |
| C8 low, all else high | You lose points socially, not technically. | Record yourself 5 times; count filler openers; force a hypothesis before every code line |
| C10 low | You over-polish. | Practice the "ugly correct in 12 minutes, then polish" contract |

interviewQuestions.text: Explain automatic fail flags and when you would use it.
Explain score bands and when you would use it.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
| # | Dimension | 1 (bad) | 3 (solid) | 5 (excellent) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | Requirements framing | Accepts the prompt verbatim | Asks functional + a couple of non-functional questions | Derives scale numbers first, then asks only the questions that change the design |
| S2 | Estimation | No numbers at all, or absurd ones | Daily actives, QPS, storage, bandwidth are all present and roughly right | Estimates are stated with the arithmetic shown, include 3× headroom, and are sanity-checked against known products |
| S3 | Capacity derivation | None | "Reads are more than writes" | Per-component write, read, and storage math derived from the entity model |
| S4 | API / interface design | No interfaces | Endpoints with payloads sketched | Contracts include pagination, idempotency, versioning, error shape, and rate limits |
| S5 | Data model | Ad-hoc, no schema | Entities and relationships identified, storage engine justified | Data model keyed by access pattern, with sharding/partitioning strategy and growth path |
| S6 | Component decomposition | Monolith blob | Clear service boundaries with a diagram | Boundaries chosen by team/domain ownership, not by noun in the prompt |
| S7 | Storage and caching strategy | "Use a database" | DB plus cache with a stated reason | Cache keys, TTLs, invalidation strategy, stampede protection, and read/write ratios |
| S8 | Consistency and transactions | Hand-wavy | Acknowledges eventual consistency where relevant | Explicit consistency boundary per operation; exactly-once or at-least-once semantics named |
| S9 | Scalability and reliability | "Add more servers" | Horizontal scaling, load balancer, replicas | Failure domains, retries with backoff, circuit breakers, degradation modes |
| S10 | Observability | "Add logs" | Metrics, logs, traces, alerting on key SLIs | SLI/SLO definitions, golden signals, what each alert pages on and who is paged |
| S11 | Security | Ignored | AuthN/AuthZ, TLS mentioned | Threat model sketch, secrets handling, rate limiting, audit trail, least privilege |
| S12 | Communication and whiteboard | No narration, no diagram | Narrates, draws a reasonable diagram | Uses the whiteboard as a tool — labels boxes, arrows, and data flow direction, keeps it legible |
| S13 | Trade-off awareness | One solution, no alternatives | Mentions one alternative and rejects it | 2–3 options with explicit criteria for choosing; says what would change the answer at 100× |

**Automatic fail flags.** No numbers by the 10-minute mark. No diagram at the 20-minute mark. Cannot name a single failure mode of their design. Solution depends on a component that fundamentally cannot work (global joins across shards with no reconciliation story).

**Score bands.** 35–65 total = strong mid. 25–34 = acceptable mid with weak spots. Below 25 = junior. Above 45 = senior. If your S1 or S5 is a 1, cap your overall at "needs a second round" regardless of the sum — interviewers use gating.

topics.description: Behavioral round scorecard within Mock Interview Scorecards.
keyConcepts: Story inventory (build this before any loop)
The reverse-question bank

interviewQuestions.text: Explain story inventory (build this before any loop) and when you would use it.
Explain the reverse-question bank and when you would use it.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
Behavioral is where offers are won and lost by candidates who ace coding. Scoring is about structure and specificity, not about having a dramatic story.

| # | Dimension | 1 (bad) | 3 (solid) | 5 (excellent) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| B1 | Structure (STAR / STARL) | Stream of consciousness, 4 minutes with no shape | Clear Situation/Task/Action/Result, 90 seconds | Tight Situation (1 sentence), clear personal ownership in Action, quantified Result, plus a Learning beat |
| B2 | Personal ownership | "We did X" the whole way through | "I did X" with some detail | "I decided X over the alternative Y because Z" — the decision and the rejected option are both visible |
| B3 | Specificity | No numbers, no names, no artifacts | One or two concrete details | Metrics before/after, the actual artifact, the timeline, the constraint that forced the design |
| B4 | Failure handling | No failure story, or blame is external | Admits a real mistake, explains the fix | Names their mistake, the detection mechanism, the fix, and the systemic change that prevented recurrence |
| B5 | Conflict handling | Avoids the question or escalates to blame | Describes a disagreement resolved by data or by deferring | Shows influence without authority, and the relationship outcome |
| B6 | Ambiguity | Only stories with a clear plan from day one | Some ambiguity, partial plan | Story where the requirements shifted mid-flight and they re-planned without a reset |
| B7 | Feedback receptivity | Defensive | Takes feedback, no example of applying it | Gives an example of applying feedback that came from a peer, manager, or user review |
| B8 | Impact orientation | Task-completion framing | "Delivered on time" | "Changed the outcome the business cared about" with the metric named |
| B9 | Brevity | Rambling, interviewer has to steer | 90–120 seconds | Under 90 seconds, lands the point, then stops |
| B10 | Reverse questions | None, or "what's the tech stack like" | One or two process questions | Questions that show you have already thought about the role's actual problems |

**Story inventory (build this before any loop).** Eight stories, each written once and rehearsed: (1) biggest technical win, (2) hardest bug, (3) a shipped failure with a postmortem, (4) a disagreement you won or lost well, (5) a time you had to learn something fast, (6) a time you mentored or unblocked someone, (7) a time you said no to a stakeholder, (8) a time you were wrong and it cost money or time. Any loop longer than 60 minutes will touch four of these.

**The reverse-question bank.** What does on-call look like for this team in the first 30 days? What is the most recent production incident and what did it change? How do you decide what not to build? What does the code review culture look like when people disagree? Where has this team been technically wrong before, and what did it cost? What is the next six months' roadmap and what is the riskiest part? What does a promotion actually require here?

topics.description: Backend round scorecard within Mock Interview Scorecards.
keyConcepts: Backend auto-fails

interviewQuestions.text: Explain backend auto-fails and when you would use it.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
| # | Dimension | 1 (bad) | 3 (solid) | 5 (excellent) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bk1 | Requirements and contract modeling | Writes handlers first, thinks about the model later | Resource model, endpoints, status codes reasonable | Contract-first design; edge and error cases enumerated before implementation |
| Bk2 | Data modeling | No schema, ORM-generated blobs | Normalized enough, FKs deliberate | Access-pattern-driven schema, explicit denormalization with a reconciliation story, migration strategy |
| Bk3 | Transaction boundaries | One giant transaction, or none | Correct boundaries for the use case | Idempotent writes, outbox/inbox for cross-service, saga for multi-service |
| Bk4 | Concurrency correctness | Lost updates, no locking strategy | Optimistic locking or atomic ops where needed | Knows isolation levels and their anomalies; picks the weakest sufficient isolation; explains race scenarios |
| Bk5 | API design quality | Verbs in paths, inconsistent errors | Resource-oriented REST, consistent error envelope | Versioning strategy, pagination contract, idempotency keys, deprecation plan |
| Bk6 | Input validation and injection | String-concatenated SQL | Parameterized queries, schema validation at the edge | Defense in depth: edge validation, DB constraints, least-privilege DB user, no dynamic SQL without a builder |
| Bk7 | AuthN/AuthZ | Auth checked "somewhere" | Correct session or token validation, per-route authz | Object-level authorization, token revocation, tenant isolation tested, privilege escalation considered |
| Bk8 | Caching | "Redis makes it fast" | Correct keys, TTL, invalidation on write | Stampede protection, negative caching, cache-aside with versioned keys, measured hit rate |
| Bk9 | Background work | Cron inside a web process | Queue with retries and DLQ | Idempotent consumers, visibility timeout correctness, ordering per key, poison message handling |
| Bk10 | Observability | console.log | Structured logs with request IDs | Tracing across services, RED metrics, business metrics, alerting tied to user impact |
| Bk11 | Async correctness | fire-and-forget promises | Awaited properly, errors handled | Concurrency limits, timeouts with abort signals, graceful shutdown draining in-flight work |
| Bk12 | Testability and tests | Integration-only | Unit plus integration, factories | Contract tests, deterministic time/randomness, test pyramid respected, migrations tested both directions |

**Backend auto-fails.** N+1 queries in a live session and no detection. Unparameterized SQL. No transaction around a multi-write mutation. Blocking call in an async handler (N+1 database round-trips in an event loop). Missing idempotency on a payment-like POST.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain devops auto-fails and when you would use it.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
| # | Dimension | 1 (bad) | 3 (solid) | 5 (excellent) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | Container fundamentals | Cannot write a Dockerfile | Multi-stage build, non-root user, sensible workdir | Correct layer ordering for cache reuse, minimal base, pinned digests, OCI-shape awareness |
| D2 | Image and build hygiene | Latest tag, huge image | Pinned versions, .dockerignore, multi-stage | Distroless/slim, SBOM, signed images, no package manager left in the final layer |
| D3 | Orchestration concepts | Pods exist | Deployments, Services, Ingress, ConfigMap, Secret | Probes configured correctly, resource requests/limits set, disruption budgets, topology spread |
| D4 | Kubernetes debugging reflex | `kubectl get pods` only | describe, logs, describe events, exec | Port-forward, ephemeral containers, metrics server, `kubectl debug node`, previous logs |
| D5 | Config and secrets | Secrets in git | Env/config maps, secret manager | Rotation, least privilege, no secret in image layers, runtime secret injection |
| D6 | Networking | Pod IP used directly | Service DNS, Ingress with TLS | NetworkPolicy default-deny, headless services, connection-draining behaviour |
| D7 | Scaling and scheduling | "Set replicas to 10" | HPA on CPU/memory, replicas for HA | Custom metrics, PDB, VPA, cluster autoscaler, cold-start vs latency trade-off |
| D8 | Deployment and rollback | Recreate only | Rolling update, readiness gate | Blue/green or canary with metric gates, automated rollback, migration compatibility strategy |
| D9 | State and storage | EmptyDir for real data | PVCs with appropriate access modes | StatefulSet with stable identity, storage class trade-offs, backup and restore actually tested |
| D10 | CI/CD | Manual deploys | Build once, promote the same artifact | Pipeline stages with gates, environment parity, secret scoping, SBOM and scan in the gate |
| D11 | IaC | Click-ops | Terraform for everything, state in remote backend | Modules, drift detection, plan review as a code-review artifact, immutable outputs |
| D12 | Observability and on-call | Dashboards nobody reads | Metrics + logs + traces, alerts on symptoms | SLIs/SLOs, error budgets, runbooks, blameless postmortems, on-call load measured |
| D13 | Cost awareness | Ignored | Right-size requests, spot for batch | Cost per request tracked, storage lifecycle policies, autoscaler tuning, waste dashboard |

**DevOps auto-fails.** Running `kubectl` against production with no context check. Deploying a migration in the same step as code that requires it, without a compatibility window. No readiness probe on a service that needs warm-up. Storing secrets in environment variables that get logged.

topics.title: The self-scoring rubric and what a "4 out of 5" actually means
topics.description: These are behaviourally anchored, so your score means the same thing on every mock.
keyConcepts: What a 4 actually means, precisely
What a 3 actually means
The calibration exercise that makes this real
Composite scoring
Trend rule, not absolute rule
The two-score rule

interviewQuestions.text: Explain what a 4 actually means, precisely and when you would use it.
Explain what a 3 actually means and when you would use it.
Explain the calibration exercise that makes this real and when you would use it.
Explain composite scoring and when you would use it.
Explain trend rule, not absolute rule and when you would use it.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Definitions.** These are behaviourally anchored, so your score means the same thing on every mock.

| Score | Label | Behavioural definition | Interview signal |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | Excellent | Handles the hard part of this problem unprompted, and explains the trade-off behind the choice | Strong hire at the next level up; strong hire here |
| 4 | Strong | Solves it with a small prompt, or solves it alone but the explanation of the trade-off is thin | Hire here; credible for a stretch |
| 3 | Solid | Solves the common case unaided; needs a nudge for the edge case or the justification | Hire at this level |
| 2 | Weak | Needs multiple prompts or a partial solution to get to correct | No hire at this level; maybe at one below |
| 1 | Absent | Cannot get traction after reasonable help | No hire |

**What a 4 actually means, precisely.** A 4 is *not* "better than average". It means: you reached the correct answer on your own trajectory, and the trajectory was reasonable. Concretely, a 4 in coding means your clarification was adequate, your data structure was right, your code was correct on all cases including edge cases, and your complexity analysis was accurate — you simply did not have a strong opinion on alternatives, or you did not volunteer the optimization. A 4 in system design means you produced a coherent design with real numbers and a defensible bottleneck discussion, but you did not proactively surface a failure mode I was hoping you would.

**What a 3 actually means.** A 3 is a hire, and you should stop feeling bad about it. It means the common case was handled cleanly and you needed help only on the edge of the problem space. Most successful mid-level candidates score 3s. The interview is not a 5-or-bust test; it is a "no 1s, no 2s in the core dimension" test.

**The calibration exercise that makes this real.** Score a recorded mock against the anchors above *before* asking anyone else to score it. Then compare. The delta is your calibration error, and calibration error is what makes you panic mid-interview ("I'm failing!") or coast ("I'm nailing this!") when you are not. Do this once a week for four weeks.

**Composite scoring.**

| Track | Weighting | Hiring threshold |
|---|---|---|
| Coding-heavy loop | Coding 60%, design 25%, behavioral 15% | Coding average ≥ 3.4, no dimension ≤ 2 |
| Design-heavy loop | Design 55%, coding 20%, behavior/deep-dive 25% | Design average ≥ 3.4, S1 and S5 ≥ 3 |
| Full product loop | Coding 35%, design 30%, behavior 20%, round-specific 15% | Weighted average ≥ 3.4, no 1s |

**Trend rule, not absolute rule.** Your interview performance is the average of your last three mocks, not your best one and not one bad afternoon. Track the composite in a spreadsheet with a date column. If three consecutive mocks are flat below threshold, you do not need more practice hours — you need to change what you practice (see K.1.2's pattern table) or you have a knowledge gap that practice cannot fix.

**The two-score rule.** Always record two numbers per mock: the score, and your *comfort* score (how calm you felt, 1–5). When scores are flat but comfort is rising, you are genuinely improving and the interview will follow. When comfort is rising but scores are flat or falling, you have overconfidence — your practice is too easy, and you must increase difficulty (harder problems, unseen topics, live people).

---

Full table
Decision flow

interviewQuestions.text: Explain class meanings and when you would use it.
Explain full table and when you would use it.
Explain decision flow and when you would use it.
Explain retry-safety rule and when you would use it.
Explain idempotency and status codes and when you would use it.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟢 Beginner · **Must-know** — you must be able to pick a code without hesitating.

**Class meanings.**

| Class | Name | Meaning | Retry? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1xx | Informational | Request received, processing continues | n/a |
| 2xx | Success | Request received and accepted successfully | n/a |
| 3xx | Redirection | Further action needed to complete the request | Follow |
| 4xx | Client error | Request cannot be fulfilled; **the caller** is at fault | Fix the request |
| 5xx | Server error | Server failed to fulfil an apparently valid request | Maybe, with backoff |

**Full table.**

| Code | Name | Use when | Interview trap |
|---|---|---|---|
| 200 | OK | Read succeeded with a body; synchronous write succeeded | Do not use for a create; use 201 |
| 201 | Created | Resource created; include `Location` header | No body required |
| 202 | Accepted | Work queued asynchronously; job not yet done | Must give a status/check URL |
| 204 | No Content | Success with nothing to return (DELETE, `PUT` that is idempotent) | Must not include a body |
| 206 | Partial Content | Range request satisfied | CDN/media only |
| 301 | Moved Permanently | Resource has a new canonical URL | Browser caches aggressively; use for domain moves |
| 302 | Found | Temporary redirect, method may change to GET in practice | Do not use for auth flows |
| 303 | See Other | Redirect that forces GET after the action | Correct for POST-then-redirect (PRG) |
| 304 | Not Modified | Cache is still valid | Must have sent `ETag` or `Last-Modified` |
| 307 | Temporary Redirect | Temporary, **method and body preserved** | Right choice for HSTS-ish and API redirects |
| 308 | Permanent Redirect | Permanent, method and body preserved | Permanent API version moves |
| 400 | Bad Request | Malformed syntax or invalid parameters the server cannot parse | Not for semantically invalid but well-formed |
| 401 | Unauthorized | **Unauthenticated** — missing or invalid credentials | The correct name is "unauthenticated"; everyone misuses it |
| 403 | Forbidden | Authenticated but **not authorized** for this action | Do not leak that the resource exists |
| 404 | Not Found | No resource at that path, or intentionally concealed | Sometimes used to hide 403 for enumeration resistance |
| 405 | Method Not Allowed | Path exists, verb does not | Must include `Allow` header |
| 406 | Not Acceptable | Cannot produce a response in the client's `Accept` | Rare in practice |
| 408 | Request Timeout | Client took too long to send | |
| 409 | Conflict | State conflict: duplicate, version mismatch, concurrent edit | Use with an `ETag`/version for optimistic locking |
| 410 | Gone | Deliberately removed, no forwarding | Preferred over 404 for deletions if you want the distinction |
| 412 | Precondition Failed | `If-Match`/`If-Unmodified-Since` failed | The optimistic-locking failure code |
| 413 | Content Too Large | Body exceeds limits | Tell the limit |
| 415 | Unsupported Media Type | Content-Type not accepted | |
| 422 | Unprocessable Content | Semantically invalid but syntactically valid | Validation failures go here; 400 for parse errors |
| 423 | Locked | Resource is locked | Rare |
| 424 | Failed Dependency | A dependency operation failed | Saga/compensation case |
| 429 | Too Many Requests | Rate limited | Must include `Retry-After` |
| 431 | Request Header Fields Too Large | Headers over limit | |
| 500 | Internal Server Error | Unhandled exception | Never leak a stack trace |
| 501 | Not Implemented | Server does not support the functionality | |
| 502 | Bad Gateway | Upstream returned garbage or connection reset | |
| 503 | Service Unavailable | Temporarily down or overloaded; `Retry-After` | The right 5xx for load shedding |
| 504 | Gateway Timeout | Upstream did not respond in time | Always pair with a client timeout |

**Decision flow.**

```
Is the request syntactically parseable?
  no  -> 400
  yes -> Is the semantics valid (schema, business rule)?
          no  -> 422
          yes -> Do we know who you are?
                  no  -> 401
                  yes -> May you do this?
                          no  -> 403
                          yes -> Does the resource exist here?
                                  no  -> 404
                                  yes -> Does the verb work?
                                          no  -> 405
                                          yes -> Did we accept it for async work?
                                                  no  -> is this a state conflict?
                                                          yes -> 409 / 412
                                                          no  -> success -> 200/201/204
                                                  yes -> 202
```

**Retry-safety rule.** Only retry idempotent methods (`GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, `DELETE`) automatically. Never auto-retry `POST` without an idempotency key. Retry `429`, `502`, `503`, `504` with exponential backoff and jitter. Never retry `400`, `401`, `403`, `404`, `422`.

**Idempotency and status codes.** An idempotency key replay that matches the original request returns the *original* response status, usually `200` or the original `201`, plus a header like `Idempotency-Key-Replayed: true`. Reusing a key with a *different* body is `409`.
