| 405 | Method Not Allowed | Path exists, verb does not | Must include `Allow` header |
| 406 | Not Acceptable | Cannot produce a response in the client's `Accept` | Rare in practice |
| 408 | Request Timeout | Client took too long to send | |
| 409 | Conflict | State conflict: duplicate, version mismatch, concurrent edit | Use with an `ETag`/version for optimistic locking |
| 410 | Gone | Deliberately removed, no forwarding | Preferred over 404 for deletions if you want the distinction |
| 412 | Precondition Failed | `If-Match`/`If-Unmodified-Since` failed | The optimistic-locking failure code |
| 413 | Content Too Large | Body exceeds limits | Tell the limit |
| 415 | Unsupported Media Type | Content-Type not accepted | |
| 422 | Unprocessable Content | Semantically invalid but syntactically valid | Validation failures go here; 400 for parse errors |
| 423 | Locked | Resource is locked | Rare |
| 424 | Failed Dependency | A dependency operation failed | Saga/compensation case |
| 429 | Too Many Requests | Rate limited | Must include `Retry-After` |
| 431 | Request Header Fields Too Large | Headers over limit | |
| 500 | Internal Server Error | Unhandled exception | Never leak a stack trace |
| 501 | Not Implemented | Server does not support the functionality | |
| 502 | Bad Gateway | Upstream returned garbage or connection reset | |
| 503 | Service Unavailable | Temporarily down or overloaded; `Retry-After` | The right 5xx for load shedding |
| 504 | Gateway Timeout | Upstream did not respond in time | Always pair with a client timeout |

**Decision flow.**

```
Is the request syntactically parseable?
  no  -> 400
  yes -> Is the semantics valid (schema, business rule)?
          no  -> 422
          yes -> Do we know who you are?
                  no  -> 401
                  yes -> May you do this?
                          no  -> 403
                          yes -> Does the resource exist here?
                                  no  -> 404
                                  yes -> Does the verb work?
                                          no  -> 405
                                          yes -> Did we accept it for async work?
                                                  no  -> is this a state conflict?
                                                          yes -> 409 / 412
                                                          no  -> success -> 200/201/204
                                                  yes -> 202
```

**Retry-safety rule.** Only retry idempotent methods (`GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, `DELETE`) automatically. Never auto-retry `POST` without an idempotency key. Retry `429`, `502`, `503`, `504` with exponential backoff and jitter. Never retry `400`, `401`, `403`, `404`, `422`.

**Idempotency and status codes.** An idempotency key replay that matches the original request returns the *original* response status, usually `200` or the original `201`, plus a header like `Idempotency-Key-Replayed: true`. Reusing a key with a *different* body is `409`.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know** — headers are 5-minute interview wins and are frequently asked cold.

**Request headers.**

| Header | Purpose | Gotcha |
|---|---|---|
| `Authorization` | Credentials: `Bearer <token>` or `Basic` | Do not log it; strip at the edge |
| `Content-Type` | Media type of the body | Drives parsing; missing means some servers reject |
| `Accept` | What response types are acceptable | Drives 406 |
| `Accept-Encoding` | Compression: `gzip, br` | Only compress above ~1 KB; small responses get bigger |
| `Accept-Language` | Locale preference | |
| `Cookie` | Browser cookies | `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite` apply |
| `Host` | Target authority | Required in HTTP/1.1 |
| `User-Agent` | Client identity | |
| `X-Request-Id` / `traceparent` | Distributed trace correlation | Propagate end to end; this is your debugging lifeline |
| `If-None-Match` | Conditional GET with ETag | Produces `304` |
| `If-Match` | Optimistic concurrency precondition | Produces `412` on mismatch |
| `Idempotency-Key` | Client-generated unique key for safe POST retries | Scope to the authenticated principal |
| `Range` | Partial content request | Backs resumable downloads |

**Response headers.**

| Header | Purpose | Gotcha |
|---|---|---|
| `Content-Type` | Media type of response | Always set; missing means clients guess |
| `Content-Length` | Body size | Conflicts with chunked encoding |
| `Content-Encoding` | Compression applied | |
| `Location` | Where the resource is / where to redirect | Required on `201` |
| `ETag` | Opaque version of the representation | Strong vs weak (`W/"..."`) |
| `Last-Modified` | Timestamp-based validator | Second granularity; coarser than ETag |
| `Cache-Control` | Cache directives | The most misused header in production |
| `Vary` | Headers that change the response | Must include anything that changes representation, or caches cross-contaminate |
| `Set-Cookie` | Sets a cookie | Flagged by interview: `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/` |
| `Retry-After` | Seconds or HTTP-date to wait | Required on `429`/`503` |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` | CORS allow-list | Never `*` with credentials |
| `Strict-Transport-Security` | Force HTTPS for a period | Only send over HTTPS |
| `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` | Do not sniff content type | Cheap XSS hardening |
| `Content-Security-Policy` | XSS mitigation policy | Tightly scoped origins, no `unsafe-inline` |
| `Referrer-Policy` | What to leak in `Referer` | `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` is a sane default |
| `X-Frame-Options` / `frame-ancestors` | Clickjacking | Use CSP `frame-ancestors` where possible |
| `Server` | Software identification | Remove; free recon for attackers |

**`Cache-Control` cheat sheet.**

| Directive | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `no-store` | Never write to any cache (secrets, PII) |
| `no-cache` | May store, must revalidate before every use |
| `private` | Only a browser may store it |
| `public` | Any cache may store it (CDN OK) |
| `max-age=60` | Fresh for 60 seconds; no revalidation within that window |
| `s-maxage=300` | Fresh 300 s for shared caches only |
| `stale-while-revalidate=60` | Serve stale for 60 s while revalidating in the background |
| `stale-if-error=86400` | Serve stale if the origin errors — good for availability |
| `must-revalidate` | Stale is never acceptable once expired |
| `immutable` | Will never change during its freshness life; content-hashed assets only |
| `public, max-age=31536000, immutable` | The correct header for hashed JS/CSS bundles |
| `no-store` on HTML or a `max-age=0, must-revalidate` shell | The common correct pattern for an app shell + hashed assets |

**ETag mechanics.** Compute an ETag from a hash of the representation, or use a version/updated-at tuple. On a conditional request with a matching `ETag`, return `304` with **no body**. `no-cache` still allows storage; `no-store` forbids it. Weak ETags (`W/`) mean "semantically equivalent, not byte-identical" — right for compressed variants.

**Security header minimum set (memorize this list).** `Strict-Transport-Security`, `Content-Security-Policy`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy`, `frame-ancestors`/`X-Frame-Options`, `Permissions-Policy`, and cookies set `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite`.

**CORS preflight, in order.** Non-simple request (method other than GET/HEAD/POST, custom headers beyond safelisted, or `Content-Type: application/json`) triggers `OPTIONS` with `Access-Control-Request-Method` and `-Headers`. Server replies with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `-Methods`, `-Headers`, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, and optionally `Access-Control-Max-Age`. Simple requests never preflight, which is why `application/json` "breaking CORS" is really "triggering preflight". Credentials require an explicit origin, never `*`. Browsers enforce CORS; servers that "ignore it" are fine for non-browser clients — CORS is a browser policy, not an authz control.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟢 Beginner · **Must-know** — this decides the whole shape of a solution.

**Growth cheat sheet.**

| n | O(log n) | O(n) | O(n log n) | O(n²) | O(2ⁿ) | O(√n) | O(n!) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 3 | 10 | 33 | 100 | 1,024 | 3 | 3.6M |
| 100 | 7 | 100 | 664 | 10,000 | 1.27×10³⁰ | 10 | — |
| 1,000 | 10 | 1,000 | 10,000 | 1,000,000 | — | 32 | — |
| 10,000 | 13 | 10,000 | 133,000 | 100,000,000 | — | 100 | — |
| 1,000,000 | 20 | 1M | 20M | 10¹² | — | 1,000 | — |

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know** — the point at which n stops being abstract. Under 10⁴ items, O(n) full scans are usually faster than clever index walks; under 10³, an in-memory structure beats a database round-trip by three orders of magnitude regardless of complexity. The interview's real question is "at what n does your choice flip?"

**Operation table — pick the structure from the access pattern, never from fashion.**

| Structure | Access | Search | Insert | Delete | Ordered | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Array / dynamic array | O(1) index | O(n) | O(1) amortized, O(n) worst | O(n) shift | Yes | Default; dense, cache-friendly |
| Linked list | O(n) index | O(n) | O(1) given node | O(1) given node | No | Rare; pointer overhead is brutal |
| Stack | O(1) push/pop | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) | No | DFS, undo, monotonic stack |
| Queue / deque | O(1) ends | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) ends | No | BFS, producer-consumer, LRU |
| Hash map | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | No | Counts, lookups, dedupe |
| Hash set | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) | No | Membership, "have I seen this" |
| Balanced BST (Red-Black / AVL / B-tree) | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | Yes | Range queries, ordered iteration, DB indexes |
| Trie | O(L) | O(L) | O(L) | O(L) | Lexicographic | Autocomplete, prefix search, IP routing |
| Heap (binary) | O(1) min/max | O(n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | Partial | Top-K, Dijkstra, merge K streams |
| B+ tree | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | Yes | Databases and filesystems |
| Skip list | O(log n) avg | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | Yes | Redis sorted sets, some concurrent maps |
| Bloom filter | — | O(1) | O(1) | — | — | Probabilistic "definitely not present" |
| Count-min sketch | — | O(1) | O(1) | — | — | Frequency estimation, heavy hitters |
| Ring buffer | O(1) | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) | No | Logs, streaming windows, throughput |

**Space-vs-time trade table.**

| Need | Cheap option | Expensive option | Flip point |
|---|---|---|---|
| Membership on a stream | Array + O(n) scan | Hash set | A handful of items |
| Frequent min/max | O(n) scan | Heap | ~100 items or a hot loop |
| Range over keys | Hash scan + sort | Balanced BST / sorted structure | The moment ranges are common |
| Ranking | Full sort O(n log n) | Heap O(n log k) | Any k ≪ n |
| Exact order-statistics | Fenwick tree O(log n) | Balanced BST | Static data — use prefix sums |

**Amortized vs worst case.** Dynamic array append is O(1) *amortized*: occasionally O(n) to double the backing store, but O(1) on average forever. Hash map operations are O(1) *expected*, degrading to O(n) under adversarial collisions (hence tree-mode thresholds in Java, `listpack`/`hash-max-listpack-entries` tunables in Redis). Interviewers like "amortized" — say the word.

**Space complexity gotchas.** Recursion depth counts. In Python, `str += x` in a loop is O(n²) — use `''.join`. Building a 10,000-element list by repeated concatenation is O(n²). Two passes over a 10M-row table is O(n) space, not O(1). Recursion plus memoization is O(n) space. Slicing copies.

**Complexity in distributed systems.** Redis `MGET` of 100 keys is one round trip (O(n) network, one syscall). 100 sequential `GET`s is 100 round trips. This is the most common real-world complexity mistake: *round-trip count* dominates asymptotic analysis once n > ~1.

**The two questions to ask before choosing.** What is the read:write ratio? What is the access pattern (by key, by range, by prefix, by top-k, by membership)? Read-heavy + by-key → hash. Read-heavy + by-range → tree. Write-heavy + unbounded → append-only log or LSM. Top-k over a stream → bounded heap. High-cardinality membership with false positives acceptable → bloom filter.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟢 Beginner · **Must-know** — all of `SELECT`, `JOIN`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, subqueries.

**Join selection table.**

| Join | Matches | Keeps unmatched left rows | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `INNER JOIN` | Both sides matching | No | The default; you want intersection |
| `LEFT JOIN` | All left + matching right | Yes, with NULLs | Enrich, or find "has no child" |
| `RIGHT JOIN` | All right + matching left | Yes | Rare; flip the tables and use LEFT |
| `FULL OUTER JOIN` | Everything | Both sides | Merging two partial datasets |
| `CROSS JOIN` | Cartesian product | — | Generating ranges, deliberate combinations, `LATERAL` |
| `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.col IS NULL` | — | — | The anti-join pattern (faster than `NOT IN`) |

**🔴 Advanced · Must-know** — the interview favorites.

| Concept | Syntax | Trap |
|---|---|---|
| Self-join | `FROM emp a JOIN emp b ON a.mgr_id = b.id` | Manager comparisons in one row |
| Cross join to unpivot | `CROSS JOIN LATERAL (VALUES ('a',a.x),('b',a.y)) AS t(k,v)` | The cleanest unpivot in Postgres |
| Lateral join | `FROM orders o, LATERAL (SELECT * FROM items WHERE order_id=o.id LIMIT 5) i` | Per-row subquery; powers top-N-per-group |
| Recursive CTE | `WITH RECURSIVE t AS (base UNION ALL recurse) SELECT ...` | Needs a depth guard or infinite recursion |
| Grouping sets | `GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((a),(b),())` | Fast subtotal matrix |
| Rollup | `GROUP BY ROLLUP(a,b)` | Hierarchical subtotals |
| Cube | `GROUP BY CUBE(a,b)` | Full subtotal matrix |
| Window function | `OVER (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b ROWS BETWEEN ...)` | Window, not aggregate — no `GROUP BY` collapse |
| `QUALIFY` (DuckDB, BigQuery, Snowflake) | `QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1` | Postgres needs a subquery wrapper |

**Window functions you must know cold.**

| Function | Returns | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `ROW_NUMBER()` | 1,2,3… no ties | Pagination, dedupe to latest |
| `RANK()` | 1,1,3 | Top-N with ties honoured |
| `DENSE_RANK()` | 1,1,2 | Same, no gaps |
| `NTILE(k)` | Bucket 1..k | Percentiles, cohorts |
| `LAG(col, n, default)` | Prior row's value | Time-series deltas |
| `LEAD(col, n, default)` | Following row's value | Funnel conversion |
| `SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY ts)` | Running total | Cumulative metrics |
| `AVG(...) OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)` | Moving average | Time-series smoothing |
| `FIRST_VALUE` / `LAST_VALUE` | Boundary values | Group first/last with correct frame |
| `PERCENT_RANK()` / `CUME_DIST()` | Relative position | Percentiles |
| `GROUP_CONCAT` / `STRING_AGG` | Concatenate group | Rollups of labels |

**Frame clauses — the trap everyone falls into.**

| Frame | Rows included |
|---|---|
| `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` | Running total from the start |
| `ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` | 7-row window (includes current) |
| `RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1' DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` | Time-based; `RANGE` includes peers with equal keys |

`ROWS` = physical rows, `RANGE` = logical by value. `RANGE` with ties includes all peer rows — which silently inflates a `SUM` when ordering by a duplicated column.

**Top-N per group, three ways.**

```sql
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) rn
  FROM orders
) SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 3;

-- 2. Correlated subquery (universal, slower)

WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders x
       WHERE x.customer_id = o.customer_id AND x.created_at > o.created_at) < 3;

-- 3. LATERAL (best plan for large n)

FROM customers c

                    WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
                    ORDER BY o.created_at DESC LIMIT 3) r;
```

```sql
FROM addresses
```

```sql
  SELECT id, manager_id, name, 1 AS depth
  FROM employees WHERE id = 42
  UNION ALL

  FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id
```

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know** — "how do you know the index helped?" is asked constantly.

**B-tree index behaviour.**

| Fact | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Stores keys in sorted order | Supports `=`, `<`, `>`, `BETWEEN`, `ORDER BY`, `LIKE 'pre%'` |
| Composite index `(a, b, c)` is sorted by a, then b, then c | Only the leading column is usable alone |
| Can do a skip scan in some engines, but never rely on it | Always design for the leading column being the filter |
| Trailing `ORDER BY` columns after an equality prefix are free | `(a, b)` serves `WHERE a=1 ORDER BY b` with no sort |
| `LIKE '%x'` cannot use it | Trigram/FTS index instead |
| Functions on the column kill it | `WHERE DATE(ts) = ...` → index `ts`, range the day |
| Casting the column kills it | `WHERE id::text = $1` → index the expression or cast the literal |
| `OR` across columns needs index merge | Often better as a `UNION ALL` of two indexed queries |
| Low cardinality column alone is a bad index | Include it after a high-cardinality prefix |

**Index types and when to reach for them.**

| Type | Best for | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| B-tree | Range, equality, ordering | Write amplification, ~log n |
| Hash | Equality only, very high write volume | No range, no ordering |
| BRIN | Huge append-only tables with natural physical order (time-series) | Tiny, but useless without correlation |
| GIN | Arrays, JSONB containment, full-text search | Slow writes |
| GiST / SP-GiST | Ranges, geometric, nearest-neighbour | Specialized |
| HNSW / IVFFlat | Vector similarity | Tunable recall/speed trade |
| Partial (`WHERE`) | Hot subset of a large table, e.g. `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` | Smaller, cheaper |
| Covering / `INCLUDE` | Index-only scans | Wider index |
| Functional / expression | `LOWER(email)`, `DATE(ts)` | Must match expression exactly in the query |
| Composite with direction | Mixed asc/desc ordering | Must match the ORDER BY direction |

**Composite index design recipe.**

1. List the equality predicates, in selectivity order (most selective first).
2. Append the range predicate columns (only the first range column is really usable).
3. Append `ORDER BY` / `GROUP BY` columns.
4. Consider adding the most frequent covering columns as `INCLUDE` (never as keys, to keep the index narrow).

Example: `WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status = ? AND created_at > ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50` → index on `(tenant_id, status, created_at DESC)`. The index is narrow, ordered, and covering for the fetch.

**Reading a plan.**

| Term | Meaning | Act when |
|---|---|---|
| Seq Scan | Full table scan | Expected for small tables; suspicious on large ones |
| Index Scan | Walk the index | Good |
| Index Only Scan | Answer from index | Ideal — but needs visibility map freshness, breaks under heavy updates |
| Bitmap Index Scan | Bitmap then heap fetch | Good for low-selectivity predicates |
| Backward Index Scan | Traverse the index in reverse | Serves `ORDER BY ts DESC` on an ASC index |
| Nested Loop | Inner loop per outer row | Good when the inner side is tiny |
| Hash Join | Build a hash table | Good for large unsorted inputs |
| Merge Join | Sorted merge | Good when both inputs are already index-ordered |
| Sort | Explicit sort node | Look for `Sort Method: quicksort` vs `external merge Disk` |
| Rows Removed by Filter | Post-filter discard | A sign of a bad index choice or a stat problem |
| `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` | Actual rows and time | Read actuals, not estimates |

**The estimate-vs-actual gap.** When the planner's estimate is off by orders of magnitude, the plan is wrong, and the usual cause is stale or missing statistics on a skewed column, or correlation between columns. Fix: `ANALYZE`/`UPDATE STATISTICS`, raise statistics targets on the column, or create extended statistics (Postgres `CREATE STATISTICS`) for correlated predicates.

**Zero-downtime index rules.** Creating a standard index takes a share lock that blocks writes. Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (outside a transaction, Postgres) or your engine's online/concurrent equivalent. Adding a `NOT NULL` or a default rewrites the table in older Postgres — prefer add-with-default-then-backfill-then-validate. Adding a foreign key takes a lock on the referencing table — add `NOT VALID` then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`.

**Common index mistakes.** Indexing low-selectivity columns. Indexing every column ("the more indexes the better" — each one slows writes). Overlapping indexes where one is a prefix of another. Indexing before you have the query. Forgetting that a `LEFT JOIN`'s right-side predicate belongs in the `ON` clause, not `WHERE`, or you will convert it to an inner join. Failing to index the foreign key used by a join or by `ON DELETE CASCADE`. Forgetting that an index does not help `COUNT(*) WHERE f(x)` if `f(x)` is not indexable.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know** — pick the data structure from the access pattern.

| Need | Structure | Core commands | Watch out |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cache a value with TTL | String | `GET`, `SET`, `SETEX`, `SETNX`, `MSET`, `MGET`, `INCR`, `INCRBY`, `DECR` | `SETEX`/`SET .. EX` should be the default, not `SET` then `EXPIRE` |
| Value presence / flags | String or Set | `EXISTS`, `SISMEMBER` | `EXISTS` returns a count |
| Counter with expiry | String | `INCR`, `INCRBY`, `INCRBYFLOAT`, `EXPIRE` | Use a Lua script or `SET NX EX` + `INCR` for correct init |
| Unique set / tags / followers | Set | `SADD`, `SREM`, `SMEMBERS`, `SISMEMBER`, `SCARD`, `SRANDMEMBER`, `SSCAN`, `SDIFF`, `SUNION`, `SINTER` | `SMEMBERS` on a huge set blocks the event loop — use `SSCAN` |
| Leaderboard / ranking | Sorted set | `ZADD`, `ZINCRBY`, `ZRANGE`/`ZRANGEBYSCORE`, `ZRANK`, `ZREVRANK`, `ZREVRANGE`, `ZCOUNT`, `ZRANGEBYLEX`, `ZPOPMIN` | Scores must be comparable across members |
| Priority queue / delay queue | Sorted set or list | `ZADD score=unix_ts`, read with `ZRANGEBYSCORE 0 now` | Poll, or push to a stream |
| Work queue | List / stream | `LPUSH`+`BRPOP`, `RPUSH`+`BLPOP`; `XADD`, `XREADGROUP`, `XACK`, `XAUTOCLAIM` | `BRPOP` blocks the connection |
| FIFO log / recent N | List | `LPUSH`, `LPUSHX`, `LTRIM`, `LRANGE`, `LINSERT` | Cap with `LTRIM key 0 999` |
| Pub/sub fanout | Pub/sub channel | `PUBLISH`, `SUBSCRIBE`, `PSUBSCRIBE` | Fire-and-forget; messages are lost if subscribers are down |
| Durable queue | Stream | `XADD`, `XREAD`, `XGROUP CREATE`, `XREADGROUP`, `XACK`, `XPENDING`, `XAUTOCLAIM`, `XTRIM MAXLEN ~` | Consumer groups give at-least-once + pending list |
| Distributed lock | String + Lua | `SET key val NX PX ttl`, `EVAL` unlock, `SET key val XX PX` | Redlock is contentious; add a fencing token or use a real broker |
| Rate limiter | String + Lua or token bucket | `INCR` + `EXPIRE`, `GET`+`SET`, GCRA via Lua | Fixed window bursts at boundaries; prefer sliding window |
| Session store | Hash / String | `HSET`, `HGET`, `HSETEX`, JSON blob with TTL | Set TTL on the hash, not just fields |
| IP / geo lookup | Sorted set + Geo | `GEOADD`, `GEOSEARCH`, `GEODIST` | Geo sets are zsets under the hood |
| HyperLogLog | HLL | `PFADD`, `PFCOUNT`, `PFMERGE` | ~0.81% error; not exact, not mergeable across deletes |
| Bloom filter | Module or bitmap in String | `BF.ADD`, `BF.EXISTS` / `SETBIT`, `GETBIT` | No deletion in classic bloom |
| Lock-free unique job | `SET NX` | Same as distributed lock | Needs TTL |
| Multi-attribute lookup | Hash | `HGET`, `HMGET`, `HSCAN` | Good for partial reads of a wide object |

**TTL and eviction.**

| Command | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `TTL key` / `PTTL key` | Remaining seconds / ms |
| `EXPIRE key s` / `PEXPIREAT key ts-abs` | Set TTL |
| `EXPIREAT key ts-abs` | Expire at a wall-clock time |
| `PERSIST key` | Remove TTL |
| `SET key v EX 60 NX` | Atomic set with TTL and conditional |
| `SETEX key 60 v` | Atomic set with TTL (legacy but fine) |

**Eviction policies.** `noeviction` (fail writes — correct for a primary store), `allkeys-lru`, `volatile-lru`, `allkeys-random`, `volatile-ttl`. LFU variants (`allkeys-lfu`) protect hot keys better. Eviction means your cache is a lie under memory pressure — never store a session or a queue in an `allkeys-lru` instance.

**Transactions and scripting.** `MULTI/EXEC` batches commands but gives **no isolation** from other clients — commands are queued, then run in order, and nothing is rolled back on error. `WATCH`+`MULTI` gives optimistic locking (abort on a watched key changing) and has the ABA-ish caveats of long-held watches. `EVAL` a Lua script for atomic read-modify-write; scripts must be deterministic and must not block — this is why long-running work in a script will stall the single-threaded server.

**Cluster and replication facts worth stating.** Redis is single-threaded for command execution, so any O(n) command is a latency incident for the whole instance (hence `SCAN`, not `KEYS`; `UNLINK`, not blocking `DEL` on huge keys; `SLOWLOG GET`). Replication is asynchronous → replication lag, and a failover can lose acknowledged writes. `WAIT` can give a stronger durability acknowledgement. Cluster shards by hash slot across 16384 slots; multi-key operations only work within a slot, which is why people use hash tags `{user42}` to co-locate keys. Sentinel provides automatic failover for a primary/replica setup; Cluster does sharding plus failover.

**Anti-patterns to name proactively.** Cache without a TTL. `KEYS *` in production. Storing large blobs instead of object references. Read-through vs write-through confusion (prefer cache-aside: app reads cache, on miss reads DB and populates). Nondeterministic cache keys (including the user agent). Single-flight missing, so a hot key expiry causes a stampede — fix with a short randomized TTL jitter or a distributed lock around repopulation.

| Counter with expiry | String | `INCR`, `INCRBY`, `INCRBYFLOAT`, `EXPIRE` | Use a Lua script or `SET NX EX` + `INCR` for correct init |
| Unique set / tags / followers | Set | `SADD`, `SREM`, `SMEMBERS`, `SISMEMBER`, `SCARD`, `SRANDMEMBER`, `SSCAN`, `SDIFF`, `SUNION`, `SINTER` | `SMEMBERS` on a huge set blocks the event loop — use `SSCAN` |
| Leaderboard / ranking | Sorted set | `ZADD`, `ZINCRBY`, `ZRANGE`/`ZRANGEBYSCORE`, `ZRANK`, `ZREVRANK`, `ZREVRANGE`, `ZCOUNT`, `ZRANGEBYLEX`, `ZPOPMIN` | Scores must be comparable across members |
| Priority queue / delay queue | Sorted set or list | `ZADD score=unix_ts`, read with `ZRANGEBYSCORE 0 now` | Poll, or push to a stream |
| Work queue | List / stream | `LPUSH`+`BRPOP`, `RPUSH`+`BLPOP`; `XADD`, `XREADGROUP`, `XACK`, `XAUTOCLAIM` | `BRPOP` blocks the connection |
| FIFO log / recent N | List | `LPUSH`, `LPUSHX`, `LTRIM`, `LRANGE`, `LINSERT` | Cap with `LTRIM key 0 999` |
| Pub/sub fanout | Pub/sub channel | `PUBLISH`, `SUBSCRIBE`, `PSUBSCRIBE` | Fire-and-forget; messages are lost if subscribers are down |
| Durable queue | Stream | `XADD`, `XREAD`, `XGROUP CREATE`, `XREADGROUP`, `XACK`, `XPENDING`, `XAUTOCLAIM`, `XTRIM MAXLEN ~` | Consumer groups give at-least-once + pending list |
| Distributed lock | String + Lua | `SET key val NX PX ttl`, `EVAL` unlock, `SET key val XX PX` | Redlock is contentious; add a fencing token or use a real broker |
| Rate limiter | String + Lua or token bucket | `INCR` + `EXPIRE`, `GET`+`SET`, GCRA via Lua | Fixed window bursts at boundaries; prefer sliding window |
| Session store | Hash / String | `HSET`, `HGET`, `HSETEX`, JSON blob with TTL | Set TTL on the hash, not just fields |
| IP / geo lookup | Sorted set + Geo | `GEOADD`, `GEOSEARCH`, `GEODIST` | Geo sets are zsets under the hood |
| HyperLogLog | HLL | `PFADD`, `PFCOUNT`, `PFMERGE` | ~0.81% error; not exact, not mergeable across deletes |
| Bloom filter | Module or bitmap in String | `BF.ADD`, `BF.EXISTS` / `SETBIT`, `GETBIT` | No deletion in classic bloom |
| Lock-free unique job | `SET NX` | Same as distributed lock | Needs TTL |
| Multi-attribute lookup | Hash | `HGET`, `HMGET`, `HSCAN` | Good for partial reads of a wide object |

**TTL and eviction.**

| Command | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `TTL key` / `PTTL key` | Remaining seconds / ms |
| `EXPIRE key s` / `PEXPIREAT key ts-abs` | Set TTL |
| `EXPIREAT key ts-abs` | Expire at a wall-clock time |
| `PERSIST key` | Remove TTL |
| `SET key v EX 60 NX` | Atomic set with TTL and conditional |
| `SETEX key 60 v` | Atomic set with TTL (legacy but fine) |

**Eviction policies.** `noeviction` (fail writes — correct for a primary store), `allkeys-lru`, `volatile-lru`, `allkeys-random`, `volatile-ttl`. LFU variants (`allkeys-lfu`) protect hot keys better. Eviction means your cache is a lie under memory pressure — never store a session or a queue in an `allkeys-lru` instance.

**Transactions and scripting.** `MULTI/EXEC` batches commands but gives **no isolation** from other clients — commands are queued, then run in order, and nothing is rolled back on error. `WATCH`+`MULTI` gives optimistic locking (abort on a watched key changing) and has the ABA-ish caveats of long-held watches. `EVAL` a Lua script for atomic read-modify-write; scripts must be deterministic and must not block — this is why long-running work in a script will stall the single-threaded server.

**Cluster and replication facts worth stating.** Redis is single-threaded for command execution, so any O(n) command is a latency incident for the whole instance (hence `SCAN`, not `KEYS`; `UNLINK`, not blocking `DEL` on huge keys; `SLOWLOG GET`). Replication is asynchronous → replication lag, and a failover can lose acknowledged writes. `WAIT` can give a stronger durability acknowledgement. Cluster shards by hash slot across 16384 slots; multi-key operations only work within a slot, which is why people use hash tags `{user42}` to co-locate keys. Sentinel provides automatic failover for a primary/replica setup; Cluster does sharding plus failover.

**Anti-patterns to name proactively.** Cache without a TTL. `KEYS *` in production. Storing large blobs instead of object references. Read-through vs write-through confusion (prefer cache-aside: app reads cache, on miss reads DB and populates). Nondeterministic cache keys (including the user agent). Single-flight missing, so a hot key expiry causes a stampede — fix with a short randomized TTL jitter or a distributed lock around repopulation.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟢 Beginner · **Must-know** — losing work in Git is an interview-day catastrophe as well as a career one.

**Daily commands.**

| Task | Command | Note |
|---|---|---|
| What is my state right now | `git status -sb` | Read this first, always |
| What did I change | `git diff`, `git diff --staged` | `git diff --staged --stat` for review |
| Stage | `git add -p` | Patch mode; review hunk by hunk |
| Stage everything I meant | `git add -A` then `git diff --staged` | Never blind-add in a repo with secrets |
| Unstage | `git restore --staged <file>` | Also: `git reset` (mixed) |
| Commit | `git commit -m "..."` | Imperative mood, explain *why* |
| Amend last commit | `git commit --amend --no-edit` | Only for unpushed commits |
| Undo staged, keep file | `git restore <file>` | |
| Undo last commit, keep changes staged | `git reset --soft HEAD~1` | |
| Undo last commit, keep changes unstaged | `git reset HEAD~1` | |
| Undo last commit, discard changes | `git reset --hard HEAD~1` | Nuclear; check `git stash list` first |
| Recent history, one line | `git log --oneline --graph --decorate -20` | |
| Who changed this line | `git blame -L 40,60 <file>` | Also `git log -S"string" -p` |
| Find when a string appeared | `git log -S"foo" --oneline`, `git log -G"regex" -p` | Gold for "when did this break" |
| Which branches contain a commit | `git branch -a --contains <sha>` | |
| Compare branches | `git diff main...feature` | Three dots = changes on feature only |
| Search across history | `git log --all -p -S"error_code"` | Slow but definitive |
| Show a file at a past commit | `git show <sha>:<path>` | |
| Binary search for the breaking commit | `git bisect start`, `git bisect bad`, `git bisect good <sha>`, `git bisect run <script>` | The most underused power tool |
| Find which local branch has this commit | `git log --all --oneline --source | grep sha` | |
| List my worktrees | `git worktree list` | Great for parallel tasks |
| Clean untracked files | `git clean -nd` (dry run!) then `git clean -fd` | Always dry-run |

**The five recovery situations.**

| Situation | Command | Explanation |
|---|---|---|
| Wrong commit message | `git commit --amend` | Only unpushed |
| Wrong changes committed | `git reset --soft HEAD~1` then re-stage | Keeps everything |
| Uncommitted junk to park | `git stash push -u -m "wip"` / `git stash pop` / `git stash list` | `-u` includes untracked |
| Want yesterday's version of a file | `git restore --source=HEAD~1 -- <file>` | Without staging |
| Need to return a deleted file | `git checkout <sha> -- <file>` or `git restore --source=<sha> -- <file>` | |
| Branch got too messy | `git rebase -i HEAD~20`, `squash`/`fixup`/`reword`/`drop`, then `git rebase --continue` | History rewrite, only before PR |
| Force push rejected | `git fetch`, then `git rebase` instead of `--force-with-lease` | Prefer `--force-with-lease` over `--force` |
| Need the reflog | `git reflog` | Every movement of `HEAD`; `HEAD@{1}` = previous position |
| Rescue a lost commit after a bad reset | `git reflog` → find the sha → `git reset --hard <sha>` or `git branch rescue <sha>` | **This is why you never run `git gc` manually** |
| Conflict | `git status` → fix files → `git add` → `git rebase --continue` / `git merge --continue` | During a rebase: `git rebase --abort` to bail |
| Want to abandon a rebase/merge | `git rebase --abort`, `git merge --abort` | |
| Detached HEAD panic | `git switch -c my-branch` | Your commits are safe; just branch |
| Wrong remote, right local | `git remote -v`, `git remote set-url origin <url>` | |

**Pull strategies.**

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `git pull` | Fetch + merge (or rebase if configured) |
| `git pull --rebase` | Linear history; rebases your local commits on top of upstream |
| `git fetch` then inspect | Always prefer this before any risky operation |
| `git fetch --prune` | Drop deleted remote branches |
| `git push --force-with-lease` | Safe force push; fails if someone else pushed |
| `git push --set-upstream origin feature` | First push of a branch |
| `git push origin --delete feature` | Delete a remote branch |

**Interview-relevant facts.** A commit is a pointer to a tree, a tree is a directory snapshot, and a parent pointer makes history a DAG — hence rebases are copies, not moves, which is why force-push is needed. `HEAD` is a symbolic ref to a branch; detached `HEAD` points directly at a commit. Index (staging area) is a third tree. The reflog is per-ref, local, and survives for ~90 days. `.gitignore` only affects untracked files; already-tracked files stay tracked — `git rm --cached`. `git bisect` needs ~log₂(n) steps, so 1,000 commits is 10 steps.

**Never do these on an interview machine.** `git reset --hard` before committing, `git clean -fd` without `-n`, `git push --force` to a shared branch, `git rebase` a branch someone else is on, or `git config --global` anything you cannot undo.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟢 Beginner · **Must-know** — writing a Dockerfile and debugging layers live.

**Command reflex table.**

| Goal | Command | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Build | `docker build -t name:tag .` | Context is the last arg; `.dockerignore` matters |
| Build no cache | `docker build --no-cache -t name:tag .` | |
| Multi-platform | `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t name:tag --push .` | |
| Run | `docker run -d -p 8080:8080 --name app name:tag` | |
| Run with env | `docker run --env-file .env -e LOG_LEVEL=debug ...` | |
| Run a shell | `docker run -it --rm name:tag sh` | `--rm` or you accumulate junk |
| Exec in a running container | `docker exec -it <id> bash` | |
| Logs | `docker logs -f --tail 100 <id>` | `--since 10m`, `-t` for timestamps |
| List | `docker ps`, `docker ps -a`, `docker images` | |
| Stop / remove | `docker stop`, `docker rm -f`, `docker system prune` | Never `system prune -a --volumes` blindly |
| Inspect | `docker inspect <id>`, `docker inspect -f '{{.State.Health.Status}}' <id>` | |
| Resource usage | `docker stats` | |
| Shell into a crashed container | `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh name:tag` | When there is no shell, use the entrypoint override |
| Port mapping and DNS | `--expose`, `-p host:container`, `--network` | On a user-defined network, containers resolve by name |
| Volume | `-v host:/path`, `--mount type=volume,src=x,dst=/path` | `--mount` is more explicit and less surprising |
| Env at runtime | `-e`, `--env-file` | Never `ENV` a secret — it is baked into layers |
| User | `--user 1000:1000`, `--read-only` | Defence in depth |
| Health | `--health-cmd`, `--health-interval` | Or the `HEALTHCHECK` directive |
| Compose | `docker compose up -d --build`, `logs -f`, `down -v` | `-v` deletes volumes; it deletes data |
| Registry | `docker login`, `tag`, `push`, `pull` | |
| Resource limits | `--memory`, `--cpus`, `--memory-swap` | Must match what the app expects |
| See a container's writes | `docker diff <id>` | Great for "why is my data gone" |
| Debug a compose service | `docker compose exec svc sh` | |

**Dockerfile directives.**

| Directive | Purpose | Rule of thumb |
|---|---|---|
| `FROM` | Base image | Pin a version, ideally a digest; `alpine` for small binaries, `-slim`/`distroless` for production |
| `RUN` | Build-time command | Separate layers that change often from those that don't; combine to avoid leaving build tools behind |
| `CMD` | Default command/args | Overridable; prefer exec-form (JSON array) so signals work |
| `ENTRYPOINT` | Fixed entry binary | Also exec-form, so PID 1 is your app and it gets `SIGTERM` |
| `ARG` | Build-time variable | Not available at runtime; avoid secrets here too |
| `ENV` | Persisted environment variable | Appears in `docker inspect` and in the image config — never put secrets here |
| `COPY` | Copy files | Copies from build context; prefer over `ADD` (no auto-extraction surprises) |
| `ADD` | Copy, plus URL fetch and auto-extract | Use only when you want tar extraction |
| `WORKDIR` | Sets cwd and creates it | Use absolute paths; avoids `RUN cd` layers |
| `USER` | Run as non-root | Set it, and make sure your app can read what it needs |
| `VOLUME` | Declares a mount point | Usually an anonymous volume — surprising, avoid |
| `EXPOSE` | Documents the port | Does **not** publish it; purely metadata |
| `HEALTHCHECK` | Container health probe | Compose/k8s can use it |
| `LABEL` | Metadata | Keep provenance here (version, commit sha, build date) |
| `SHELL` | Sets the default shell for `RUN` | Set to `["/bin/bash","-o","pipefail","-c"]` when using pipes |

**Good multi-stage Node example.**

```dockerfile
FROM node:20-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci

FROM deps AS build
COPY . .
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev

FROM node:20-slim AS runtime
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
USER node
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/package.json ./
EXPOSE 8080
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]
```

**Layer-caching order.** Dependency manifests → install → copy source → build. Copy the source last so a one-line code change does not invalidate the dependency layer. Put `apt-get update` and `apt-get install` in the *same* `RUN`, and `rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*` in it too.

**Signal handling.** `CMD ["npm", "start"]` makes npm PID 1 and it will not forward `SIGTERM` reliably; exec the binary directly. In k8s, that is the difference between a graceful shutdown and a `SIGKILL` after 30 s.

**Production hardening checklist.** Non-root user. Read-only root filesystem with a writable volume or `tmpfs` for `/tmp`. Drop all capabilities except what is needed. `--no-new-privileges`. A healthcheck. No secrets in build args or layers. Pinned base image digest, scanned, with an SBOM. `.dockerignore` including `.git`, `node_modules`, `.env`, and build output.

**Common failure modes.** Port bound but nothing listening (`EXPOSE`/`-p` semantics). Wrong host, so it works locally and not in a container. Hostname vs `localhost` — in a container, `localhost` is the container. Missing env at runtime. Volume shadowing the app's files. Out of memory killed with exit 137 (increase limit or reduce concurrency). Exit 143 = `SIGTERM` (graceful shutdown path).

**Signal handling.** `CMD ["npm", "start"]` makes npm PID 1 and it will not forward `SIGTERM` reliably; exec the binary directly. In k8s, that is the difference between a graceful shutdown and a `SIGKILL` after 30 s.

**Production hardening checklist.** Non-root user. Read-only root filesystem with a writable volume or `tmpfs` for `/tmp`. Drop all capabilities except what is needed. `--no-new-privileges`. A healthcheck. No secrets in build args or layers. Pinned base image digest, scanned, with an SBOM. `.dockerignore` including `.git`, `node_modules`, `.env`, and build output.

**Common failure modes.** Port bound but nothing listening (`EXPOSE`/`-p` semantics). Wrong host, so it works locally and not in a container. Hostname vs `localhost` — in a container, `localhost` is the container. Missing env at runtime. Volume shadowing the app's files. Out of memory killed with exit 137 (increase limit or reduce concurrency). Exit 143 = `SIGTERM` (graceful shutdown path).

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know** — the reflexes matter more than the YAML depth.

**Core objects.**

| Object | Purpose | Key fields to know |
|---|---|---|
| `Pod` | Smallest deployable unit; one or more containers | `containers`, `resources.requests/limits`, `restartPolicy`, `nodeName` |
| `Deployment` | Declarative replicaset management + rollout | `replicas`, `strategy`, `selector`, `template` |
| `ReplicaSet` | Underlying replica controller | Rarely created by hand |
| `StatefulSet` | Stable identity + ordered rollout + per-pod PVC | `serviceName`, `volumeClaimTemplates`, `podManagementPolicy` |
| `DaemonSet` | One pod per node | Node selectors, tolerations |
| `Job` | Runs to completion | `completions`, `parallelism`, `backoffLimit` |
| `CronJob` | Scheduled Job | `schedule`, `concurrencyPolicy`, `historyLimit` |
| `Service` | Stable virtual IP + DNS | `type` (ClusterIP/NodePort/LoadBalancer), `selector`, `port`/`targetPort` |
| `Ingress` | HTTP(S) routing into the cluster | `rules`, `host`, TLS, ingress class |
| `ConfigMap` | Non-secret config | `data`, mounted as files or env |
| `Secret` | Credentials | Same shapes, plus type; base64 is *not* encryption |
| `PersistentVolumeClaim` | Request for durable storage | `accessModes`, `storageClassName`, `resources.requests.storage` |
| `ServiceAccount` | Pod identity for the API server | Bound to `Role`/`RoleBinding` |
| `Role` / `ClusterRole` / bindings | RBAC | `rules`, verbs, resources, resourceNames |
| `NetworkPolicy` | L3/L4 allow/deny | Default-deny everything, then allow |
| `IngressClass` / `Gateway` | Traffic entry | Gateway API is the successor direction |
| `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` | Scale on metrics | `minReplicas`, `maxReplicas`, metrics, behaviour |
| `PodDisruptionBudget` | Voluntary-drain safety | `minAvailable` or `maxUnavailable` |
| `ResourceQuota` / `LimitRange` | Namespace governance | |

**The debugging reflex ladder.**

```bash
kubectl get pods -n ns -o wide            # what exists, and node/restart count
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n ns          # Events at the bottom tell you 90% of it
kubectl logs <pod> -n ns                 # current container
kubectl logs <pod> -n ns --previous       # crashed container: the real answer
kubectl get events -n ns --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].state}'
kubectl exec -it <pod> -n ns -- sh        # live inspection
kubectl port-forward svc/<svc> 8080:80 -n ns
kubectl debug pod/<pod> -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot   # ephemeral container
kubectl cp <pod>:/path ./local -n ns
kubectl top pods -n ns                    # needs metrics-server
kubectl get hpa -n ns
```

**The imagePullBackOff / CrashLoopBackOff ladder.** `describe pod` for the reason (`ErrImagePull`, `ImagePullBackOff`), verify the tag exists, verify `imagePullSecrets` and the ServiceAccount, check the node's disk (`kubectl describe node`), then `kubectl get events`. For CrashLoop: `logs --previous` first, then `kubectl run tmp --image=<same image> --restart=Never --command -- sleep 3600` to reproduce outside the probes. Probe failures are usually the crash cause, not the solution: a slow app fails the readiness probe, gets killed, and restarts forever.

**Resources and scheduling.** Requests drive scheduling and the guaranteed share; limits cap usage and cause throttling (CPU) or OOM kill (memory). Always set both. Too-tight CPU limits produce latency spikes at low utilization. Use `nodeSelector`, `tolerations`/`affinity`, `topologySpreadConstraints`, and `PodDisruptionBudget` for resilience. `kubectl drain` respects a PDB; `--force --ignore-daemonsets` bypasses it, which is exactly when you get paged.

**Probes, precisely.** Startup: gates liveness/readiness until the app is warm. Liveness: restart the container if dead — never make it depend on downstream services. Readiness: remove from the Service if not ready — safe to check dependencies. Startup prevents liveness from killing a slow boot. Probe thresholds matter more than the probe type: set `initialDelaySeconds`/`failureThreshold` for your actual start-up time, not a guess.

**Service types.** ClusterIP (internal only), NodePort (node:port), LoadBalancer (cloud-provisioned, may cost money), Headless (`clusterIP: None` — StatefulSet discovery). `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` preserves the client IP and only routes to node-local endpoints — required for correct client IPs, at the cost of uneven load. Session affinity (`sessionAffinity: ClientIP`) is a band-aid; prefer stateless apps plus external session storage or a signed cookie.

**NetworkPolicy, default-deny first.** Start by denying all ingress and egress in the namespace, then add explicit allows. DNS egress must be allowed or every name lookup fails. A flat `Ingress` with no path prefix matches `/`-prefixed paths; `pathType: Prefix` versus `Exact` matters for exact routes.

**Contexts and safety.** `kubectl config current-context` and `kubectl config use-context` before anything destructive. `kubectl diff` before `apply`. `--dry-run=server` validates against the real API. `kubectl apply -f -` from stdin keeps no stray file. Never `kubectl delete --all` without quoting the namespace. `kubectl get pods --all-namespaces` to find stragglers.

**Helm reflex.** `helm install/upgrade --set key=value`, `--values values-prod.yaml`, `helm get values`, `helm history`, `helm rollback <rel>`, `helm template` to see the rendered manifests before applying. Know that a `helm upgrade` reuses the last release's values unless you pass `-f` again, and that a failed hook blocks the upgrade.

topics.title: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC vs tRPC
topics.description: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC vs tRPC within Mock Interview Scorecards.
keyConcepts: Decision guide to state out loud
Choose REST for public APIs, cacheable content, resource-oriented CRUD, third-party consumers, and file uploads.

Choose GraphQL when many different clients need different slices of a rich graph, the view count is high, and over-fetching is measurable pain. Budget for N+1 mitigation, persisted queries, and a real caching story.
Choose gRPC for internal service-to-service communication where both ends are controlled, especially for streaming, low-latency, high-volume, polyglot backends, and contract-first enforcement.

Choose tRPC when the whole app is TypeScript and you want end-to-end types with no schema duplication and no separate codegen step — you give up an external contract language and browser streaming niceties.
tRPC specifics worth naming
Versioning and evolution
Common traps to preempt

interviewQuestions.text: Explain decision guide to state out loud and when you would use it.
Explain trpc specifics worth naming and when you would use it.
Explain versioning and evolution and when you would use it.
Explain common traps to preempt and when you would use it.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know** — the answer is always "it depends", so know the dependencies.

| Dimension | REST (HTTP/JSON) | GraphQL | gRPC | tRPC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Transport | HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 | HTTP, usually POST | HTTP/2 | Depends on adapter; HTTP-focused |
| Payload shape | Fixed per endpoint | Client-specified | Fixed per RPC | Fixed per procedure |
| Over-fetch / under-fetch | Common | Solved by design | Solved by codegen | Solved by design |
| Caching | Excellent: URLs, CDN, `ETag` | Awkward: mostly POST, needs persisted queries | Limited; HTTP/2 proxy caching is poor | Endpoint-level caching |
| Batching | Awkward | Native (one query, many fields) | Native (unary batch RPCs) | Native batching |
| Latency overhead | Parsing JSON, HTTP/1.1 head-of-line | Query parse/validate/plan per request | Binary, HTTP/2 multiplexing → lower | Minimal |
| Strong typing | Weak (OpenAPI documents, does not enforce) | Schema-defined | Protobuf = enforced, versioned | End-to-end inferred types |
| Codegen and tooling | Low cost, low enforcement | High cost: schema-first or spec-first | Excellent: `protoc` generates clients/servers | Excellent: types inferred from the router |
| CORS / browser use | Native | Native (one endpoint, simpler) | Needs grpc-web + proxy | Native |
| Introspection/discovery | OpenAPI / `OPTIONS` | Introspection, ideal for tooling | Reflection | Type inference in IDE |
| Ecosystem / hiring | Universal | Large, opinionated | Strong in backend/infra, awkward for browsers | Best in a single-language full-stack TS app |
| N+1 risk | Yes, across requests | Yes, but inside one request — needs DataLoader | Same risk, per RPC | Same risk |

**Decision guide to state out loud.**

- Choose **REST** for public APIs, cacheable content, resource-oriented CRUD, third-party consumers, and file uploads.
- Choose **GraphQL** when many different clients need different slices of a rich graph, the view count is high, and over-fetching is measurable pain. Budget for N+1 mitigation, persisted queries, and a real caching story.
- Choose **gRPC** for internal service-to-service communication where both ends are controlled, especially for streaming, low-latency, high-volume, polyglot backends, and contract-first enforcement.
- Choose **tRPC** when the whole app is TypeScript and you want end-to-end types with no schema duplication and no separate codegen step — you give up an external contract language and browser streaming niceties.

**tRPC specifics worth naming.** Procedures are `query`, `mutation`, `subscription`; `t.rpc.post.create.input(zodSchema)` makes the input the single validation source, shared by client and server. Batch links coalesce multiple calls in a tick into one request. Superjson lets you pass `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `BigInt`, and `undefined` over the wire. Non-HTTP adapters exist (WebSocket, tRPC-over-anything via `httpBatchLink` vs `httpLink` vs `httpSubscriptionLink`).

**Versioning and evolution.** REST: URL path (`/v1`) for coarse major versions; additive changes only, never repurpose a field's meaning; `Sunset` header plus a documented deprecation date. gRPC: never renumber a field, always use new numbers, reserve deleted field numbers, never reuse tag numbers. GraphQL: additive fields are free and non-breaking, removing or changing one is breaking, deprecate with `@deprecated(reason:)`. tRPC: change the input schema and let the type error tell you all the callers.

**Common traps to preempt.** "GraphQL replaces REST" — no, they coexist (REST for webhooks, file upload, public API; GraphQL for your first-party clients). "gRPC is faster because binary" — mostly lower payload size and multiplexing; measure before rewriting. "REST is RESTful if it uses JSON" — no, the constraint is the resource/URI/verb model and statelessness. "tRPC is just GraphQL" — no, tRPC is not a spec, it is a library convention, so third-party consumers need your type definitions.

---

**Definition:** Four ways to express a service boundary, differing in what the contract is (a document, a schema, a schema, or TypeScript types), how it travels, and who can consume it.

| Dimension | REST | GraphQL | gRPC | tRPC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Contract** | OpenAPI document; optional, drifts without CI | Type schema (SDL); the central artifact, usually code-first or schema-first | `.proto` with generated code; strict and versioned | TypeScript types; inferred from the server, no separate artifact |
| **Transport** | HTTP/1.1 or 2, JSON (or others) | HTTP, usually `POST` with a JSON body | HTTP/2 with length-prefixed protobuf framing (see **PHASE 7**) | HTTP with JSON; batching optional; links GET for non-batched queries |
| **Who shapes the response** | Server, per endpoint | **Client**, within the schema | Server, per method | Server, per procedure (but the client is generated from the same types) |
| **Caching** | **First class.** `GET` + `ETag` + `Cache-Control` + CDN. Unbeatable | Hard. `POST` is uncacheable; `GET` needs persisted queries (5.5.10) | Not cacheable (HTTP/2 POST semantics); caches in the app or with a proxy | Limited: non-batched queries can be `GET`; batching uses `POST`; response headers usable |
| **Over/under-fetching** | Common; fixed per endpoint | Solved by design | Solved by per-method DTOs (verbose) | Solved by a procedure per need, but only if you add one |
| **Tooling** | Excellent: curl, Postman, every proxy, OpenAPI generators, docs sites | Mature: Apollo, GraphiQL, codegen, Hive/GraphOS; fewer proxies understand it | Excellent: grpcurl, reflection, Envoy, generated stubs in 10+ languages | Good within TS; limited outside it |
| **Learning curve** | Lowest | Highest (schema design, resolver map, N+1, cost analysis, client cache) | Medium-high (protobuf, HTTP/2, code generation) | Low for TS developers; the abstractions are simple |
| **Code reuse** | Types hand-maintained or shared from a package | Types shared via the schema; client codegen per platform | Generated stubs in every language from one `.proto` | **Perfect within TypeScript** â€” one type, both ends, refactor-safe |
| **N+1 risk** | Low (explicit, visible per endpoint) | **High by default**; DataLoader mandatory | Low (one call per method) | Low (one call per procedure); a nested `include` can reintroduce it |
| **Type safety** | Depends on discipline; OpenAPI + linting helps | Schema-level; variables typed by the schema; nullability enforced | **Strongest** â€” compile-time in both directions, no drift possible | **Strongest in TS** â€” compile-time, and the client is generated from the server |
| **Non-TS clients** | Any language, trivially | Any language with a client or a plain HTTP call | Excellent (official codegen everywhere) | **Not a first-class citizen** â€” you would call the HTTP endpoint by hand |
| **Public/third-party API** | **Best choice.** Documented, cacheable, universal | Poor choice without an allowlist and cost controls | Rarely exposed publicly (needs a HTTP/JSON gateway) | Rarely â€” no independent SDK story for other languages |
| **Service-to-service, latency-critical** | Good, but verbose and chatty | Rarely (loses caching) | **Best choice** â€” HTTP/2 multiplexing, low overhead, streaming | Good within one monorepo; not across languages |
| **Real-time** | SSE, WebSocket (separate protocol) | Subscriptions over WebSocket, native to the model | **Bidirectional/server-streaming/client-streaming, first class** | Subscriptions via a WebSocket adapter |
| **Best fit** | Public APIs, CRUD, cacheable reads, mixed-language consumers | Many clients with different data needs, mobile apps, aggregation across services | Internal service-to-service RPC, low latency, polyglot | TypeScript monorepo, full-stack apps, fast-moving internal APIs |

**The honest conclusion: there is no best.** REST wins on universality and caching. GraphQL wins on client flexibility and round trips, and pays for it with a query planner and a schema-governance burden. gRPC wins on internal latency and contract strength, and loses on the public web. tRPC wins on type safety inside a TypeScript codebase and has no story outside one. The genuinely good answer is to use more than one, and to choose per boundary:
- **Public/third-party** â†’ REST with a published OpenAPI contract.
- **Web/mobile frontend** â†’ a BFF, or GraphQL when the client team genuinely needs query flexibility.
- **Service-to-service** â†’ gRPC, or REST if the team is small and polyglot.
- **Internal full-stack TypeScript** â†’ tRPC.

**Questions**
1. Which one wins on caching, and why?
2. Where is N+1 most likely?
3. What is tRPC's disqualifying limitation?
4. Where is gRPC the right answer?
5. What is the strongest "use more than one" answer?

**Model answer, Q5:** "Context: an interview where I have to recommend an API style for a company with a public marketplace API, a React web app, a Swift app, and about fifteen internal services. Decision: a different style per boundary, and I would say so explicitly rather than picking one. Reasoning: the constraints at each boundary are genuinely different, so a single choice is a sign the analysis was not done. The public marketplace API serves unknown third-party clients who need documentation, real HTTP semantics, ETags, and CDN caching, so it is REST with a published, diffed OpenAPI contract. The web and mobile apps both render multi-source screens, so they sit behind a BFF for the web app â€” one team owns the composition of upstream services, and it is a simple, cacheable, cheap-to-debug contract â€” and, if the mobile team needs to combine screens differently, GraphQL for mobile specifically, because that is where the round-trip saving is real and where the client is first-party and its query shapes are reviewable. The internal services, mostly TypeScript with a couple of Go ones, use gRPC where latency matters and REST for the rest, because the operational cost of a protobuf toolchain is real and the latency requirement is not universal. Reasoning that a team of three should not run three API styles is fair, so I would sequence it: REST everywhere, then introduce one of the others where a measured constraint demands it. Trade-offs: multiple styles mean multiple sets of skills, tooling, and observability, and a developer has to know which is which. Failure scenario: a company adopts GraphQL everywhere 'for consistency', then discovers their public API clients cannot use it, their internal Go services now need a GraphQL client they have to write, and the CDN cache hit rate on their product catalogue drops from 92% to zero â€” the consistency was worth less than the specialisation."

**Mistakes:** picking one style for the whole company; using gRPC for a public API; using GraphQL for a public API with unknown clients; reaching for tRPC when non-TS consumers exist; assuming gRPC caching can be solved at the CDN; claiming GraphQL removes N+1.

**Mini task:** design the same three operations (list with pagination, get with authorization, create with idempotency) in all four styles. Then write the decision memo for a specific fictional company with two public, two internal-TS, and one Go consumer, and defend it in 200 words.

---

**Common traps to preempt.** "GraphQL replaces REST" — no, they coexist (REST for webhooks, file upload, public API; GraphQL for your first-party clients). "gRPC is faster because binary" — mostly lower payload size and multiplexing; measure before rewriting. "REST is RESTful if it uses JSON" — no, the constraint is the resource/URI/verb model and statelessness. "tRPC is just GraphQL" — no, tRPC is not a spec, it is a library convention, so third-party consumers need your type definitions.

---

**Definition:** Four ways to express a service boundary, differing in what the contract is (a document, a schema, a schema, or TypeScript types), how it travels, and who can consume it.

| Dimension | REST | GraphQL | gRPC | tRPC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Contract** | OpenAPI document; optional, drifts without CI | Type schema (SDL); the central artifact, usually code-first or schema-first | `.proto` with generated code; strict and versioned | TypeScript types; inferred from the server, no separate artifact |
| **Transport** | HTTP/1.1 or 2, JSON (or others) | HTTP, usually `POST` with a JSON body | HTTP/2 with length-prefixed protobuf framing (see **PHASE 7**) | HTTP with JSON; batching optional; links GET for non-batched queries |
| **Who shapes the response** | Server, per endpoint | **Client**, within the schema | Server, per method | Server, per procedure (but the client is generated from the same types) |
| **Caching** | **First class.** `GET` + `ETag` + `Cache-Control` + CDN. Unbeatable | Hard. `POST` is uncacheable; `GET` needs persisted queries (5.5.10) | Not cacheable (HTTP/2 POST semantics); caches in the app or with a proxy | Limited: non-batched queries can be `GET`; batching uses `POST`; response headers usable |
| **Over/under-fetching** | Common; fixed per endpoint | Solved by design | Solved by per-method DTOs (verbose) | Solved by a procedure per need, but only if you add one |
| **Tooling** | Excellent: curl, Postman, every proxy, OpenAPI generators, docs sites | Mature: Apollo, GraphiQL, codegen, Hive/GraphOS; fewer proxies understand it | Excellent: grpcurl, reflection, Envoy, generated stubs in 10+ languages | Good within TS; limited outside it |
| **Learning curve** | Lowest | Highest (schema design, resolver map, N+1, cost analysis, client cache) | Medium-high (protobuf, HTTP/2, code generation) | Low for TS developers; the abstractions are simple |
| **Code reuse** | Types hand-maintained or shared from a package | Types shared via the schema; client codegen per platform | Generated stubs in every language from one `.proto` | **Perfect within TypeScript** â€” one type, both ends, refactor-safe |
| **N+1 risk** | Low (explicit, visible per endpoint) | **High by default**; DataLoader mandatory | Low (one call per method) | Low (one call per procedure); a nested `include` can reintroduce it |
| **Type safety** | Depends on discipline; OpenAPI + linting helps | Schema-level; variables typed by the schema; nullability enforced | **Strongest** â€” compile-time in both directions, no drift possible | **Strongest in TS** â€” compile-time, and the client is generated from the server |
| **Non-TS clients** | Any language, trivially | Any language with a client or a plain HTTP call | Excellent (official codegen everywhere) | **Not a first-class citizen** â€” you would call the HTTP endpoint by hand |
| **Public/third-party API** | **Best choice.** Documented, cacheable, universal | Poor choice without an allowlist and cost controls | Rarely exposed publicly (needs a HTTP/JSON gateway) | Rarely â€” no independent SDK story for other languages |
| **Service-to-service, latency-critical** | Good, but verbose and chatty | Rarely (loses caching) | **Best choice** â€” HTTP/2 multiplexing, low overhead, streaming | Good within one monorepo; not across languages |
| **Real-time** | SSE, WebSocket (separate protocol) | Subscriptions over WebSocket, native to the model | **Bidirectional/server-streaming/client-streaming, first class** | Subscriptions via a WebSocket adapter |
| **Best fit** | Public APIs, CRUD, cacheable reads, mixed-language consumers | Many clients with different data needs, mobile apps, aggregation across services | Internal service-to-service RPC, low latency, polyglot | TypeScript monorepo, full-stack apps, fast-moving internal APIs |

**The honest conclusion: there is no best.** REST wins on universality and caching. GraphQL wins on client flexibility and round trips, and pays for it with a query planner and a schema-governance burden. gRPC wins on internal latency and contract strength, and loses on the public web. tRPC wins on type safety inside a TypeScript codebase and has no story outside one. The genuinely good answer is to use more than one, and to choose per boundary:
- **Public/third-party** â†’ REST with a published OpenAPI contract.
- **Web/mobile frontend** â†’ a BFF, or GraphQL when the client team genuinely needs query flexibility.
- **Service-to-service** â†’ gRPC, or REST if the team is small and polyglot.
- **Internal full-stack TypeScript** â†’ tRPC.

**Questions**
1. Which one wins on caching, and why?
2. Where is N+1 most likely?
3. What is tRPC's disqualifying limitation?
4. Where is gRPC the right answer?
5. What is the strongest "use more than one" answer?

**Model answer, Q5:** "Context: an interview where I have to recommend an API style for a company with a public marketplace API, a React web app, a Swift app, and about fifteen internal services. Decision: a different style per boundary, and I would say so explicitly rather than picking one. Reasoning: the constraints at each boundary are genuinely different, so a single choice is a sign the analysis was not done. The public marketplace API serves unknown third-party clients who need documentation, real HTTP semantics, ETags, and CDN caching, so it is REST with a published, diffed OpenAPI contract. The web and mobile apps both render multi-source screens, so they sit behind a BFF for the web app â€” one team owns the composition of upstream services, and it is a simple, cacheable, cheap-to-debug contract â€” and, if the mobile team needs to combine screens differently, GraphQL for mobile specifically, because that is where the round-trip saving is real and where the client is first-party and its query shapes are reviewable. The internal services, mostly TypeScript with a couple of Go ones, use gRPC where latency matters and REST for the rest, because the operational cost of a protobuf toolchain is real and the latency requirement is not universal. Reasoning that a team of three should not run three API styles is fair, so I would sequence it: REST everywhere, then introduce one of the others where a measured constraint demands it. Trade-offs: multiple styles mean multiple sets of skills, tooling, and observability, and a developer has to know which is which. Failure scenario: a company adopts GraphQL everywhere 'for consistency', then discovers their public API clients cannot use it, their internal Go services now need a GraphQL client they have to write, and the CDN cache hit rate on their product catalogue drops from 92% to zero â€” the consistency was worth less than the specialisation."

**Mistakes:** picking one style for the whole company; using gRPC for a public API; using GraphQL for a public API with unknown clients; reaching for tRPC when non-TS consumers exist; assuming gRPC caching can be solved at the CDN; claiming GraphQL removes N+1.

**Mini task:** design the same three operations (list with pagination, get with authorization, create with idempotency) in all four styles. Then write the decision memo for a specific fictional company with two public, two internal-TS, and one Go consumer, and defend it in 200 words.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know** — expect "how do you test X?" for anything.

| Level | What you are proving | Tooling examples | Frequency | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Unit | A pure function or small module behaves correctly, including edges | Jest, Vitest, pytest, `go test`, Rust built-in | Very high | Milliseconds |
| Component | A UI piece behaves correctly from the user's perspective | Testing Library, Vitest + jsdom, Playwright CT | High | Tens of ms |
| Integration | Real components talk correctly — DB, queue, HTTP handler, ORM | Testcontainers, `supertest`, `@testcontainers/postgresql`, test DB | Medium | Seconds |
| Contract | Producer and consumer agree; external API backward compatibility | Pact, Schemathesis, Dredd, OpenAPI diff | Medium, at boundaries | Seconds |
| End-to-end | The critical user journeys work in a real browser | Playwright, Cypress | Low, on the top ~10 flows | Minutes |
| Visual regression | UI rendering has not drifted | Playwright snapshots, Percy, Chromatic | Low, on components | Slow, flaky-prone |
| Load / performance | The system meets latency and throughput targets | k6, Artillery, Gatling, JMeter | Pre-release, and after big changes | Minutes |
| Property-based | Invariants hold across many generated inputs | fast-check, Hypothesis, `proptest` | Cheap to add, very high yield | Fast |
| Mutation | The tests actually detect bad code | Stryker, mutmut | Occasionally | Slow |
| Chaos / resilience | The system degrades the way you claimed | Chaos Mesh, Gremlin, manual fault injection | Quarterly | n/a |

**How to choose in an answer.** "Unit tests for logic, integration tests for anything crossing a boundary (DB, HTTP, queue), E2E only for the flows that would lose us money or customers. I aim for fast feedback on a small change, and a small number of tests that would have caught the last three incidents."

**Testing anti-patterns to name.** Asserting on implementation details instead of behaviour. Snapshot tests as a substitute for assertions (they fail for irrelevant changes and pass for wrong code). Mocking the thing under test. Mocking the database and calling it an integration test. Shared mutable state between tests, which makes them order-dependent. Arbitrary sleeps instead of awaiting a condition. Asserting a count when you should assert a specific value. 100% coverage as a goal — coverage is a smell detector, not a target.

**Determinism hygiene.** Inject a clock; use a fake timer or a controllable `now`. Seed randomness, or never test randomness directly. Give every test its own database transaction that you roll back, or a fresh container per suite. Never depend on test execution order. Clean up external state (files, queues) in `afterEach`/`teardown`.

**A concrete test that shows seniority.** Table-driven boundary tests for the pure function. A single integration test that proves the handler + repository + real Postgres agree on a transaction rollback. A property-based test asserting an idempotent operation returns the same result twice. A load test asserting p99 latency at 2× expected peak. A contract test that fails when a shared schema changes. That portfolio tells a story about how you think about risk.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know** — say numbers before you draw anything.

**Latency budget (order of magnitude, and know what dominates).**

| Operation | Typical | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| CPU instruction | ~1 ns | Reference unit |
| L1 cache read | ~1 ns | |
| L3 cache read | ~10–40 ns | |
| Main memory (RAM) read | ~50–100 ns | NUMA effects matter |
| SSD random read | ~100 µs | NVMe is 10× better than SATA |
| HDD seek | ~5–10 ms | The reason SSDs replaced them |
| Same-datacenter TCP round trip (RTT) | ~0.1–0.5 ms | 100 µs–500 µs |
| Cross-AZ within a region | ~1–2 ms | |
| Cross-region RTT | ~30–100 ms | Design implication: no synchronous cross-region writes |
| Cross-continent RTT | ~150–250 ms | |
| DNS lookup (cached) | ~0–1 ms | |
| TLS handshake (full, with TLS 1.3) | ~1–2 RTT | Session resumption is ~1 RTT; 0-RTT has replay risk |
| HTTP request → response, warm server | ~10–50 ms | |
| Cold start (Lambda-style) | ~100 ms–2 s | Pre-warming trades cost for latency |
| Postgres indexed lookup | ~1–5 ms | |
| Redis GET | ~0.2–1 ms | |
| Disk fsync | ~0.5–5 ms | Depends on storage class |

**Storage arithmetic.**

| Quantity | Formula | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Rows per day | DAU × actions/user/day | 1M DAU × 20 = 20M rows/day |
| Raw row size | Sum of columns + overhead | 500 B |
| Bytes/day | Rows/day × row size | 20M × 500 B = 10 GB/day |
| Bytes/year | Bytes/day × 365 | 3.65 TB/year |
| With replicas ×3 | ×3 | 11 TB/year |
| With index overhead (1.3–2×) | ×1.5 | |
| Text/JSON-heavy rows | 5–20 KB each | Compress with TOAST/columnar before panicking |
| Photos | Explicitly store metadata in the DB, bytes in object storage | |
| Videos | Stream, never proxy through your app | |

**Cheap row-size arithmetic.** A row with an 8 B id, 4 × 50 B strings, a 8 B timestamp, and overhead is roughly 300–500 B. Round to 500 B, sanity-check by dividing a known table's size by `pg_class.reltuples`.

**Bandwidth arithmetic.**

| Quantity | Formula | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Data in/out per request | Payload × QPS | 50 KB × 2,000 req/s = 100 MB/s = 800 Mbps per direction |
| Monthly egress | Daily × 30 | 2.7 TB/month |
| Images: thumb vs original | Resize before storing/serving | 4 KB vs 4 MB = 1000× |
| Log volume per request | ~1–5 KB | 2,000 req/s × 2 KB = 4 MB/s = 288 GB/day |
| Metrics cardinality warning | Label count is a series count | >10k active series per metric family gets expensive fast |

**Storage class trade-offs (numbers to quote qualitatively).**

| Class | Latency | Durability | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hot | ms | Multi-AZ, 11 nines | Active data |
| Warm | tens of ms | 3-4 AZ | Infrequently accessed |
| Cold | ms, retrieval-time | Single AZ | Archive |
| Glacier / archive | minutes to hours | Cheap | Legal retention, deep backup |

**Availability nines.**

| Target | Downtime/year | Downtime/day | Downtime/month | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 90% | 3.65 days | 2.4 h | 7.2 h | Free-tier hobby |
| 99% ("two nines") | 3.65 days/year | 86.4 s | 43.2 min | Internal tool |
| 99.9% ("three nines") | 8.76 hours/year | 8.64 s | 43.2 min/month | Good SaaS baseline |
| 99.95% | 4.38 hours/year | 4.32 s | 21.6 min/month | Paid-tier product |
| 99.99% ("four nines") | 52.6 minutes/year | 43.2 s | 4.32 min/month | Contractual SLA class |
| 99.999% ("five nines") | 5.26 minutes/year | 0.43 s | 26.3 s/month | Carrier-grade; very expensive |
| 99.9999% ("six nines") | 31.6 seconds/year | 0.26 ms | 0.26 s/month | Effectively impossible for many stacks |

**Availability math.** Availability = product of component availabilities. Five 99.9% components in a required chain = 0.999⁵ = 99.501%. That is why designs need redundancy and why removing a serial dependency (cache, replica read) is worth more than hardening anything.

**Error budgets.** Budget = (1 − SLO) × total time. At 99.9% over 30 days: 43.2 minutes. Budget exhausted → freeze features and spend on reliability. Budget remaining → ship faster. This reframes the reliability/speed argument as a budget conversation.

**Queue math.** If 2,000 writes/s arrive and consumers process 1,500/s, the backlog grows 500/s → 43.2M items/day → catch-up time at full capacity grows forever. Capacity planning is: consumers ≥ peak arrival rate × 1.3, plus lag alerting. Little's law: concurrency = arrival rate × latency; 1,000 req/s at 50 ms needs ~50 concurrent in-flight requests.

**QPS from users.** 1M DAU × 30 requests/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 347 req/s average. Peak is typically 2–4× average, so plan peak ≈ 1,400 req/s. Instantaneous peak is higher; autoscaling reacts in minutes, so keep headroom or use a burst-tolerant design.

**Scaling thresholds to quote.** One server handles roughly 1k–10k req/s for a trivial response, ~100–1,000 req/s for a database-backed API, and ~10–100 req/s for a heavy per-request computation — these vary enormously, so frame them as "measure, then decide", with the ratios that actually matter: CPU-bound vs I/O-bound (I/O-bound means you scale by concurrency, not CPU), and whether the database is the first bottleneck (almost always).

Explain the practical consistency choices and when you would use it.
Explain strategies to buy consistency where you need it and when you would use it.
